entries.title: Susan Collins Goes After Democrat Troy Jackson’s Anti-Abortion Record
entries.summary: “I would point out that there's only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that's me,” the Maine Republican said.
entries.content:
Since Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022, Democrats have been the ones to go after Republicans for their anti-abortion records on the campaign trail.

That did not exactly happen in Tuesday’s Maine Senate debate.

Democratic candidate Troy Jackson pressed Republican Sen. Susan Collins on whether she regretted her vote to confirm now-Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court in 2018 after he voted to overturn Roe v. Wade four years ago. But Collins fought back.

“First of all, when I evaluate Supreme Court justice nominees, I always look at their qualifications, their experience, whether they're fit to serve on the court,” Collins responded. “I clearly don't agree with how Brett Kavanaugh voted on Roe v. Wade.”

She then added: “I would point out that there's only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that's me.”

During his time in the Maine State Senate, Jackson supported some anti-abortion bills, including one to give legal standing to a fetus in the event of an attack on a pregnant patient, and another to require a 24-hour waiting period before a patient can get an abortion. In 2012, he reportedly identified himself as anti-abortion in a questionnaire administered by Project Vote Smart and said that public funding should not go to abortion.

“I would point out that it’s Troy who, until 2013, supported such extreme positions that he would not allow exceptions for a woman to have an abortion, even if her life were at stake or in cases of rape and incest,” Collins said.

While Jackson has recently said that he was “wrong on the issue” and that he now supports abortion access, he did not directly comment in the debate on his voting record supporting restrictions.

“I mean, Brett Kavanaugh was against abortion when she met with him, she knew that was going to happen, and now after it's been overturned, she doesn't regret the vote,” Jackson, appearing to stumble, said when the moderator asked if he wanted to respond to Collins.

Collins said that Kavanaugh “should not have said [Roe v. Wade] was settled law” during his confirmation hearing, “because, to me, that meant that it would not be overturned, but to be fair, you cannot ask a nominee how he might vote on some hypothetical future case.”

The Maine Republican is one of only two Senate Republicans who support abortion rights, along with Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska. Collins has led and supported legislation aimed at increasing abortion access, and was one of only three Republicans to vote against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut funding for Planned Parenthood for a year.

entries.title: Collins and Jackson Trade Blame on High Costs in Maine Senate Debate
entries.summary: The Republican incumbent heralded her independence as the Democratic challenger tied her back to Trump.
entries.content:
In the first of several debates, Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, agreed that life is too expensive for Mainers. They disagreed on pretty much everything else.

“If you look at the policies that have driven up the cost of living in Maine, you have to look at Augusta,” Collins said, referencing the state’s capital where Jackson served as state Senate president.

“What we're seeing right now with affordability issues is because of Sen. Collins not being willing to stand up to Donald Trump,” Jackson responded.

That back-and-forth on affordability between the two spanned questions on housing, health care, socialism, fraud, Iran and even a recently revealed FBI investigation that looked at Collins and her office.

Collins, who is seeking her sixth term in office, touted her independence and her success as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

Democrats picked Jackson as their nominee this summer to replace Graham Platner, who dropped out after he was accused of rape.

The Cook Political Report considers the race a toss-up, though Collins has repeatedly defied political trends in winning five terms in Maine even as Republicans, including Trump, have become politically unpopular in the state.

Political committees associated with Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC have disclosed spending in every major battleground Senate race so far — besides Maine.

“I don't think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” Collins said in response to a question from the moderator about a possible visit. “I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”

The two candidates will meet three more times in the coming weeks.

A testy point Tuesday revolved around a recent ProPublica report that said the FBI had investigated claims against Collins for a pay-to-play bribery scheme with a defense contractor based on the detailed confession of the former CEO of the company. The government did not bring charges against Collins or her associates. On Tuesday, Jackson raised that reporting as fodder that Collins was unconcerned with affordability.

“[The Trump] administration dismantled the investigation,” Jackson said. “Now she votes for Donald Trump 96% of the time. I don’t owe Trump. I don’t owe the billionaires nothing.”

Collins called the accusations “completely false” and “very offensive.” She separately pushed that she’s an independent voice in Congress, saying, “I voted against my party more than any other senator on either side of the aisle.”

The candidates also repeatedly clashed over Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Collins did not ultimately vote for, although Jackson pointed out that she voted for an earlier procedural motion to advance it.

Collins said that advancing the bill helped her include provisions like the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, which she called “so important to the state of Maine.”

Jackson retorted by calling Collins “an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Soccer Players of Week 2
entries.summary: This week’s group features a left-footed freshman phenom for the Banneker boys and a two-way standout from the Bethesda-Chevy Chase girls.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

From highlight-reel goals to shutout defensive performances, a new crew of standout athletes poured in memorable outings on the soccer field. Here’s who earned All-DMV Player of the Week for boys’ and girls’ soccer:

Victoria Fenzel, Junior, Forward, Quince Orchard

Fenzel carried the offensive load for the Cougars last week in a 2-0 win over Wootton, as the junior forward scored both of her team’s goals in the victory. Her first goal was a simple tap-in. Her second, a right-footed boot that curved from right to left and nestled into the top corner of the net, was one of the best goals that Quince Orchard coach Peg Keiller has ever seen.

“As soon as she hit that ball I was like, ‘That’s going to curve in, and there’s nothing that anybody could do about it,’” Keiller said with a laugh. “That’s one thing that we’ve been trying to get her to do is take more chances, and she’s got a nice shot.”

The jaw-dropping goal was Fenzel’s sixth in her first seven games.

Franklin Fuentes, Senior, Midfielder, Northwestern

Fuentes was the hero for Northwestern in its 3-2 overtime victory over county foe DuVal last week. The senior scored two goals, including the game-winner in overtime, as the Wildcats earned their fifth victory of the season.

“We were all hyped,” Northwestern coach Victor Ramirez said. “Everybody ran onto the field and congratulated each other. … It was a hard-fought match, and we were fortunate to be able to capitalize on that opportunity.”

Ivan Ojaruega, Freshman, Forward, Banneker

Banneker earned a program-defining win last week thanks to the left foot of Ojaruega. The Bulldogs toppled Jackson-Reed, the perennial power and top seed of the DCIAA, in what coach Samer Atawneh called an “emotional and historic moment” for Banneker.

Ojaruega scored the lone goal in the 1-0 victory. He also added an assist in a 2-0 win over Cardozo earlier in the week. In Banneker’s first six games of the season, the crafty freshman has recorded two goals and four total assists.

Ziggy Powell-Moran, Senior, Goalkeeper, Whitman

The Vikings have played one of the most treacherous schedules in the DMV so far this season, and Powell-Moran has performed admirably in goal for coach Dave Greene’s team. Despite facing the likes of WCAC heavyweights Gonzaga and St. John’s, as well as several county powerhouses, Whitman has conceded just three goals.

Last week, Powell-Moran helped the Vikings to shutout victories over Bethesda-Chevy Chase and previously undefeated Clarksburg.

“I think he brings a level of comfort for the people in front of him,” Greene said. “He certainly can make saves, he’s aggressive, he knows what he’s doing. … I think he, along with the back four, have a good connection.”

Ella Sanai, Senior, Forward, Holton-Arms

Sanai has been on a heater for Holton-Arms, one of the favorites in the Independent School League. The senior forward logged seven goals and two assists in the Panthers’ last two ISL matchups against Georgetown Day and Sidwell Friends.

The latest, a 3-1 victory over the Quakers, capped a five-game September winning streak for coach Dook Kooistra’s team.

Claire Yonly, Senior, Defender, Bethesda-Chevy Chase

Yonly, a senior captain for the Barons, made her mark in a rivalry win over Whitman last week in the annual “Battle of Bethesda.” A defensive player who can also flash her offensive prowess, the Emory commit scored two goals on offense and helped pitch a shutout on defense in an eventual 4-0 win over the Vikings.

“She’s playing lights-out soccer,” coach Travis Woodruff said. “She gets to every tackle first, she outplays players that are much bigger and stronger than her, and she can shoot from 25-30 yards out.”

entries.title: Israel May Have Been Warned About Oct. 7. Biden Officials Say the U.S. Wasn’t.
entries.summary: Three years after the massacre, American officials admit they relied too much on Israel’s intelligence and assurances.
entries.content:
Recent reports suggest that Arab governments warned Israel of a looming Hamas attack prior to Oct. 7, 2023. But former Biden administration officials have told The Washington Sun that if such warnings existed, they never made their way to Washington.

Haaretz, The New York Times and The Atlantic have reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu overlooked Egyptian and Emirati alerts about an imminent attack. Netanyahu, who is seeking reelection this month, has denied the claims, saying the information is coming from his political opponents.

Former Biden administration officials said the U.S. did not receive intelligence about a potential incursion ahead of time.

“We were as surprised as the Israelis were,” said Harrison Mann, a Defense Intelligence Agency official at the time who would resign from the military in protest of President Joe Biden’s Gaza policy. Another former official said it’s “very plausible” that the Egyptians and Emiratis got wind of something and passed it along to Israel, “as they often do.”

But the former official said the relationships between Israel and regional governments are “some of the most sensitive channels in the world” because Arab countries are loath to be seen engaging with Israel. As a result, they said, the U.S. would be unlikely to get such intelligence “unless we stole it ourselves somehow.”

Brett McGurk, Biden’s chief Middle East adviser, also denied the U.S. had prior knowledge of the attack.

“We have really looked, we did not have … anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator,” McGurk told CBS News in a weekend interview. He suggested Israel should conduct an inquiry into the circumstances around the Oct. 7 attack.

Discussions about pre-attack intelligence have spurred questions about U.S. reliance on Israeli intelligence, two of the former officials told The Sun.

“The U.S. intelligence community had delegated this portfolio to Israel,” said Mann, now the associate director for campaigns and policy at the advocacy group Win Without War. “What the U.S. missed is that the Israelis were not completely surveilling Gaza.”

Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) told The Sun that “we rely too heavily on Israel rather than developing our own ability to get information."

“What that’s meant in practice is that our policy is informed by what they want us to know, and we have blind spots in the same places they do,” said Castro, a congressman since 2013 who serves on the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs committees.

Security experts in Israel and observers internationally have faulted Netanyahu for enabling Hamas’ entrenchment in Gaza between 2007 and 2023 without considering the risks involved.

Mann said Israel had become heavily focused on Lebanon, where the armed group Hezbollah — a Hamas ally — had developed significant weaponry and battlefield experience. The other former official noted that the situation was compounded by Israel’s outsize focus on gathering intelligence about Iran, to the detriment of tracking other foes.

“We can’t outsource our intelligence needs to any country, especially one that is so distracted along different fronts,” they said, describing “lackluster infrastructure” among Israeli monitoring of Gaza that “atrophied over time.”

Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vermont) tied the intelligence questions to broader concerns about the U.S.-Israel relationship.

“Congress needs answers about our over-reliance on Israeli intelligence before the October 7 attacks — as well as the quality of the intelligence Israel has provided since, especially given the tens of thousands of deadly airstrikes in Gaza that U.S. taxpayers have been forced to fund,” Welch told The Sun.

Americans’ view of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has evolved in the years since the Oct. 7 attack and Israel’s retaliation in Gaza and beyond. A rising crop of Democratic lawmakers is wary of the country. And a survey conducted in May by the Pew Research Center found a drop in the favorable view of the Israeli government among Republicans from 65% in 2022 to 51% this year. Meanwhile, other Western countries are moving to pressure Israel to address concerns about Palestinian welfare and rights.

Netanyahu formed the most far-right government in his country’s history in January 2023, then soon began shrinking Gaza’s economic ties with Israel — its lifeline, given Egypt and Israel had largely cut off the Palestinian territory from the rest of the world. Netanyahu’s administration also bolstered Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, land that would be key to eventual Palestinian statehood.

Several former Biden administration officials said the U.S. may have missed how Netanyahu’s rightward political shift — and worsening humanitarian conditions for Palestinians — could lead to desperation and, ultimately, drive violence.

I delve into those warning signs more deeply in my recently published book “Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors and Israel’s War in Gaza” (W.W. Norton, 2026). A lightly adapted excerpt follows:

Indications of a new all-out conflict grew in 2023, as income into Gaza plummeted and Israel and Palestinian Islamic Jihad–one of the strip’s armed groups–clashed in May. The flare-up killed eleven Palestinian and two Israeli civilians. The year 2023 also saw far more Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank, and Hamas claiming responsibility for Palestinian attacks inside Israel, fueling suspicions that Netanyahu would launch an offensive in both Gaza and the West Bank, and that Hamas might try to preempt him, said Mike Casey, a U.S. diplomat stationed in Jerusalem at the time. (He also eventually quit the U.S. government over its approach to Gaza.)

Casey described the Biden administration as “in denial” about the effect of U.S. support for Israel. “Come on, the IDF doesn’t participate in settler violence!” Barbara Leaf, the top Middle East official at the State Department and a former ambassador, protested to diplomats on a visit, he recalled. (Leaf did not respond to a request for comment.) In fact, analysts and human rights groups had for years agreed the Israeli military enabled attacks by Israelis who have developed settlements and outposts in the occupied West Bank in violation of international law.

Biden had granted greater autonomy to the office of Palestinian affairs at the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem, rather than fulfilling his campaign promise to re-establish an American consulate to the Palestinians. But as officials in that office issued warnings that Palestinian desperation would boil over, “We heard crickets from Washington,” Casey said.

Casey said his team issued a report days before Oct. 7 describing Gaza’s “unsustainable” economic situation. “This place is going to go off a cliff,” Casey said the memo effectively argued.

Steve Gabavics, a U.S. colonel also based in Jerusalem at the time, said he saw five American intelligence reports sent to Washington in the three months before the Hamas invasion that warned of a rising threat but were seemingly ignored.

In U.S. national security circles, it was clear the administration saw Israel-Palestine as “a managed conflict” that was unlikely to erupt in unpredictable ways, according to Mann.

When top Biden aides did consider Israeli-Palestinian peace, it was in the context of a moonshot plan for an alliance between the United States, Israel and Saudi Arabia – which involved throwing a bone to Palestinians for the sake of demonstrating Arab solidarity, and which they felt would earn them a place in history. McGurk and then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken were finalizing a draft U.S.-Saudi agreement with concessions to Palestinian demands in the days leading up to October 7. And days before the Hamas attack, then-national security adviser Jake Sullivan publicly stated that under Biden, “the Middle East region is quieter today than it has been for two decades.”

The assertion was not only inaccurate; it angered Biden administration critics from pro-Palestinian progressives to national security hawks, who noted that Sullivan and his team had done little to stem the power of Iran, a U.S. foe that armed Hamas.

Both before and following the eventual attack, Biden aides were aware of the Israeli leader’s ability to manipulate the U.S.-Israel relationship for his own interests and his cynicism, exemplified by his tacit support of Hamas’s rule in Gaza and split from the Palestinian Authority, which controls part of the West Bank.

“If anyone is most responsible for the empowerment of Hamas… it’s not [Yahya] Sinwar, it’s not [Hamas political chief Ismail] Haniyeh, it is Bibi,” a senior State Department official told me, using a nickname for Netanyahu. “Over the course of his twenty-five years in and out of office, it is the by-product of a strategy predicating on seeing to it that there was no united Palestinian governance [but] dueling power centers.”

More generally, U.S. officials were developing a better understanding of Israel’s military and intelligence capabilities – long assumed to be exemplary, and central to any retaliatory campaign against Hamas. “We were all surprised by the ineffectiveness of the Israeli defenses and by the unpreparedness on the part of Israeli intelligence," the senior State Department official told me. Israeli officials obtained and reviewed Hamas’ battle plan for October 7 more than a year before the assault but doubted it was feasible and ignored advice to prepare, a New York Times investigation found. And just weeks before the attack, the chief of intelligence for the IDF, Aharon Haliva, told his U.S. counterparts that Hamas had been “domesticated,” a top Biden aide told me.

With U.S. spies focusing on Al Qaeda and its offshoots since the 9/11 attacks, Gabavics said the CIA was “horrible” in analysis on Gaza. Well before Oct. 7, Washington had clues Israel’s capacity was exaggerated, a former U.S. intelligence official argued, saying Israeli counterparts were evasive in giving American spies access to their raw intelligence and techniques.

entries.title: Funding Cuts Aimed at Unauthorized Immigrants Are Hitting Americans, Too
entries.summary: The White House targeted a 50-year-old program for U.S. citizens and green card holders.
entries.content:
Born and raised in El Paso, Texas, Alfonso Griego says a federally funded college success program was the key for him to move forward on the path to becoming a veterinarian for farm animals.

“I would have dropped out of college,” Griego said of the program, which is only available for U.S. citizens or immigrants with green cards and has gotten bipartisan support from lawmakers for more than 50 years.

That program at El Paso Community College is one of dozens across the country facing an uncertain future after the Trump administration refused to spend money lawmakers set aside for it, part of an $800 million “pocket rescission” move that Congress' watchdog said violated the law.

Two of the programs caught in the cuts — the High School Equivalency Program, HEP, and the College Assistance Migrant Program, CAMP — were created in the late 60s and early 70s to educate migrant seasonal farmworkers and their families. While CAMP restricts participation to U.S. citizens or green card holders, HEP also allows undocumented immigrants.

The Trump administration, in announcing the cuts, cast the two programs as subsidizing “aliens to come to the U.S. and utilize our education system at the expense of American workers and their children.”

Andres Muro, who’s built HEP and CAMP at El Paso Community College over the past 25 years, said that by the end of the year approximately 40 staff members will lose their jobs and participants won’t get GED classes, and after June, first-year college students won’t have the support that helped Griego thrive.

“These are the people that feed us,” Muro said of migrant farmworkers. “Everything we put in our mouth, from myself to the president of the United States, comes from their labor.”

In the past fiscal year, 105 people enrolled to earn a GED through HEP at El Paso Community College, and 42 college students got access to mentoring, tutoring and free laptops through CAMP, Muro said.

“They are United States workers who work very, very hard to feed us, and to treat them this way, to me, is unacceptable,” Muro said.

In total, more than 70 community colleges and universities had been waiting for months for the Trump administration to choose who’d get the next round of HEP and CAMP grants. Instead, more than half of the $52 million won’t get spent, and the rest of the funds went to programs that had more time left on their five-year grants.

The National HEP-CAMP Association filed a long-shot lawsuit against the Education Department to release the funds on Sept. 30, the last day of the fiscal year. It’s the second year in a row it has had to do so. Housing groups hit in the rescissions have also sued the administration.

Last year, the Trump administration also missed the July 1 deadline to award the HEP and CAMP grants. The government only made the decision to cancel the competition for new awards on Sept. 15, 2025, nearly a month after the association sued, according to court documents.

Greg Contreras, director of CAMP at Portland Community College, said that switchup last year caused the community college to close its HEP program after 15 years. He said he’s now focused on keeping CAMP alive without a budget and enough funds for salary until the spring semester.

“They’re trying to starve us out, they’re trying to zero us out, by just frontloading a few programs, canceling the rest or defunding the rest,” Contreras said.

Students who already finished their first year are volunteering as mentors to serve the current cohort of 40 students. PCC’s CAMP recruits students from high schools serving kids whose parents work mostly in grape and blueberry farms and plant nurseries, Contreras said.

“I don't agree at all with the administration's portrayal of what they think a migrant is or what they think our programs are,” he said. “I would love for the administration to meet my students; they would see that these students want to be here in America.”

The White House rescissions package also targeted grants that funded citizenship classes for permanent residents eligible for the naturalization process. However, the Department of Homeland Security canceled that program in March 2025.

That freezing of the Citizenship and Integration Grant Program prompted backlash from dozens of Democratic lawmakers, who demanded U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services reinstate it. Congress had funded the grants since 2009.

The rescissions announcement labels the integration grants as Biden-era programs that “laundered taxpayer dollars to radical open borders NGOs who provided legal services to illegal aliens.” It named the National Partnership for New Americans as an example.

Nicole Melaku, NPNA’s executive director, said she was surprised the organization was named on the list because their grant ended in 2024.

“It's a blatant mischaracterization of our work,” Melaku said. “They named us as an open borders group, that is simply not what we do. NPNA, for years, has advocated for access to citizenship for lawful permanent residents.”

USCIS had previously touted the grant as helping more than 350,000 immigrants prepare to become citizens. But for the second Trump administration, a 75% drop in naturalizations is a victory.

Solutions in Hometown Connections in the D.C. metro area had a two-year grant for the integration program that ended in September 2025. Merritt Groeschel, the founder and executive director, said SHC has been able to continue providing classes but has scaled back other services through funds from the Greater Washington Community Foundation.

“Our students are in class saying that their dream is to be a U.S. citizen, and you want to take that away,” Groeschel said. “That is such a good thing about the United States. I just find it really sad.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: 'A Serious Red Flag'
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 7, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The Capital-less capital, an anti-AV protest and more parking tickets.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 10/10. Legit candidate for nicest day of the year! Sunshine and Goldilocks highs around 70 to 75.Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

“We’re not looking at D.C. It’s a serious red flag.”

That’s what three national banks told Kimberly Driggins when she courted them for investment this past week, the affordable housing executive said yesterday at a panel hosted by the D.C. Policy Center.

“We are sort of the last place right now that people want to do a deal,” said Driggins, the chief executive officer of the Washington Housing Conservancy. “[Lenders] are looking in the DMV, but it's Maryland and Virginia.”

Each panelist pointed to the same reason why: D.C. landlords are struggling with “sustained and systemic non-payment” of rent, as Hilary Allard Goldfarb of the Rockefeller Group put it.

Until the council can figure out how to help landlords collect — and therefore beat back a national perception that D.C. is “leading the country” in drawing out eviction cases — the Democratic nominee for mayor should reevaluate her publicly stated goal of building 72,000 housing units within five years, Driggins said.

“Maybe we need to rethink that number,” she said. “I think we need to focus on preserving what we have — there's a lot of affordable housing here that is at risk of being lost.”

But Janeese Lewis George isn’t backing off that goalpost. Though her campaign acknowledged the District’s “serious economic challenges” including nonpayment, Lewis George’s communications director said that their team is working with the private sector to restore confidence in D.C.’s housing market.

“D.C. needs to build more homes in more neighborhoods. That’s a fact. To get there, we have to stabilize the market, preserve the affordable housing we already have, and get on top of the rental arrears challenges while protecting our tenants. Those priorities go hand in hand,” Amanda Michelle Gomez, the communications director, wrote in a statement shared with The Sun. “72,000 homes is an ambitious goal because it should be.”





DEEP DIVE

Pump the brakes: A coalition of rideshare drivers, religious leaders and union workers rallied yesterday outside the Wilson Building to protest a council bill that would green-light autonomous vehicle companies’ operation in the District.

Their chief concern was job losses, citing recent data that shows trips per hour and gross hourly pay for rideshare drivers falls in cities where AVs operate.

“The job situation in this city has already been compromised and hurt by this federal administration,” William Young, who is the pastor at Covenant Baptist United Church of Christ and attended the rally, told The Washington Sun. “So many residents in Ward 8 have to take on jobs as Uber, Lyft drivers just to make ends meet. This is an extra burden on them.”

Inside the Wilson Building, Ward 6 council member Charles Allen — who chairs D.C.’s transportation committee — pointed out that D.C.’s proposed law differs from other cities in that it’ll set aside a portion of the fines and fees AV companies pay for rideshare drivers.

“No other jurisdiction has this, where dollars are literally set aside to help workers that may be facing some type of displacement,” Allen told reporters.





FROM THE DISTRICT

More parking tickets may be on the way. The D.C. Council on Tuesday approved a bill that will allow business groups and universities to hire off-duty D.C. parking enforcement officers to write tickets. Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau says it’s a means to address parking scofflaws in popular areas, but At-Large council member Robert White complained that it would instead make life more expensive for residents. He offered an amendment that would halve all D.C. parking fines, but it didn’t pass over cost concerns.

Take less initiative, D.C. The council also passed a bill that will impose new restrictions on ballot initiatives, the city’s only tool allowing residents to pass laws themselves. Proponents say the bill is meant to give the public more input into proposed initiatives, while critics argue that it’s actually an underhanded way to curtail direct democracy in D.C.

A federal judge declined to reinstate Jacqueline Smith as ombudsman for U.S. military newspaper Stars and Stripes — but did not outright dismiss her case, which claims her firing was a violation of her First Amendment rights, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

The question of whether Thomas Jefferson fathered children with the enslaved half-sister of his late wife may be settled after a DNA test was run on a single hair found on the former president’s handmade Bible, The Washington Post reports. The results point to a 99.9% certainty that Jefferson was the father of at least one of her children.

Lawyers for ex-Olympian David Hearn, who was charged by the Justice Department with intentionally damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, have called on inspectors general to probe what led to the Interior and Justice departments’ “shocking and indefensible treatment” of their client, The Associated Press reports.

The Department of Justice asked a federal judge yesterday to shut down Rep. Joyce Beatty’s attempt to force the government to provide communications between President Donald Trump and Kennedy Center officials, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports.





FROM MARYLAND

The Sphere National Harbor, planned to be a mini version of the famed orb-shaped venue in Las Vegas, is projected to generate 4,150 construction jobs. But there’s no guarantee any of those positions will go to unionized workers after the Prince George’s County Council shot down two proposals that would have secured 40% of construction jobs for the project for local unions, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For bookworms: Beyond the Book Bans: The Samuels Public Library Story, Thursday.

For porch partiers: Capitol Hill Porchfest, Saturday.

For conscious costumers: Costume Swap at the SPARK! Art Market, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

The Mystics officially play in the smallest arena in the WNBA. The Atlanta Dream announced they’ll begin playing all of their home games atState Farm Arena in 2027, writes The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri. They were the only team with a smaller home venue than the Mystics. That leaves the Mystics as a fairly extreme outlier in the WNBA: CareFirst Arena, which seats 4,200 in Southeast D.C., is less than half the size of the next smallest.

entries.title: The Commanders’ Pass Rush Is Starting to Make an Impact
entries.summary: Washington created a number of disruptive plays on defense last week, which could be pivotal this Sunday against the Giants.
entries.content:
There’s no such thing as moral victories in football. The Commanders know that better than just about any other team in the NFL this season.

You were one two-point conversion from tying the Eagles in Week 1? Good job. You put up spirited efforts with your second- and third-string quarterbacks in double-digit losses to the Cowboys and Colts, respectively? Someone get the banners ready!

That being said, the Washington defense cleaned up a weakness on Sunday versus Indianapolis that had been one of the causes for them being one of the lower-ranked defenses in the NFL — and it could pay dividends in Sunday’s pivotal divisional matchup with the Giants.

The revamped pass rush had not been creating the kind of pressure and disruption through three games that is needed to make defensive coordinator Daronte Jones’ scheme click. Instead, quarterbacks have carved up the secondary to the tune of 242.5 yards per game, the eighth-highest total in the league.

But that all changed on Sunday in London, with the pass rush causing havoc in the form of two sacks, a forced fumble and an interception. That in turn forced the Colts to either make quarterback Daniel Jones get the ball out faster or, in the case of the fourth quarter, abandon the passing game altogether.

The defense got things going right out of the gate. On the first play from scrimmage, linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson and defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw bull-rushed their blockers nearly into Jones, whose first reads Laquon Treadwell and Josh Downs were covered in the secondary. Jones then decided to dump off to running back Jonathan Taylor in the flat, but Kinlaw got his hands up and swatted the ball down.
Commanders Pass Rush 1 (1376x764, AR: 1.80)On the very next play, linebacker Odafe Oweh joined the bull rush party, pushing Bernhard Raimann into Jones’ lap. The quarterback again tried to find Taylor in the flat, but tripped over Raimann in the process and fumbled the ball into Oweh’s hands.
Commanders Pass Rush 2 (1376x758, AR: 1.82)For the entirety of the first half it was more of the same for the defense: get into Jones’ face and force him into a decision he doesn’t want to make. Whether it was lineman Dorance Armstrong overpowering right tackle Jalen Travis or linebacker Frankie Luvu getting a free lane on a blitz, there were few minutes for Jones to sit in a clean pocket and make throws.

What started as tips or throws into the dirt eventually turned into interceptable passes.

Halfway through the first quarter, Chaisson and defensive tackle Daron Payne stunt-rushed left guard Quenton Nelson and Raimann. The offensive lineman couldn’t recover from the switch, which forced Jones to have to rush his downfield throw to Treadwell across the middle. The pass was too high for Treadwell and nearly fell into the hands of cornerback Fabian Moreau.
Commanders Pass Rush 3 (1376x764, AR: 1.80)Jones wasn’t as lucky in the second quarter. On 3rd and 10, Armstrong bull-rushed through Travis and dove for Jones as he was getting into his throwing motion. At the same time, Payne powered through a double team by center Tanor Bortolini and guard Matt Goncalves. To avoid the rush, Jones threw off his back foot, but sailed the pass over receiver Ashton Dulin — instead hitting cornerback Rasul Douglas in stride for an interception.

The Commanders defense didn’t force a turnover through the first two weeks in part due to its inability to generate this type of pressure on opposing quarterbacks. Washington has forced five turnovers the past two weeks.
Commanders Pass Rush 4 (1371x768, AR: 1.79)In the second half, the Colts wisened up. They added more protection for Jones and had him getting the ball out quicker to negate the Commanders rush. And by the fourth quarter, they all but abandoned the pass despite holding just a narrow lead. (Knowing that Washington’s offense was limited on account of being down to their third-string quarterback, rookie Athan Kaliakmanis, probably factored into the decision.)

But next week’s opponent, the Giants, might not have the same luxury. Not only is it expected that starter Jayden Daniels will return from the dislocated elbow he suffered in Week 2, but New York’s running game has been pedestrian, with running back Cam Skattebo averaging 3.5 yards per carry (the eighth-worst rate in the NFL).

If the Giants choose instead to let offense run through backup quarterback Jameis Winston, there’s an opportunity for the Commanders to make the type of game-changing plays that limited Jones on Sunday — especially if Washington turns up the heat on Winston.

The veteran quarterback has a reputation for pushing the ball downfield, and with that comes a tendency to hold onto the ball. He has taken an average of three sacks per game so far this season since taking over for injured starter Jaxson Dart, tied for the third-highest rate in the league. That means there should be ample opportunity for the Commanders to get after Winston and recreate some of the pass-rush success they had in London.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Remember Maine?
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The Collins-Jackson debates have begun. Tom Emmer tells us what the midterms are about. How Republicans went on offense on health care. An unlikely crusader against Citizens United. And: New reporting on how the Biden administration responded to Oct. 7.





THE LATEST

Is this still the Maine event? Remember when all anyone could talk about was the Maine Senate race? Last night, incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins shared a debate stage with her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson.

He held his own, staying largely on his message that Collins voted to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court and that she’s a member of the same party as Donald Trump. Collins stuck to her message, too, reminding voters that she’s a powerful appropriator every chance she got. When she wasn’t saying that, she was pointing out her own votes against Trump agenda items.

Mainest moment: When the candidates debated who had closer ties to Canada, Collins mentioned a sister-in-law north of the border; Jackson said, “I’m partly French!”

If none of these pitches got the job done, the candidates have three more debates coming up, including one tomorrow night.

Democrats would love to win Maine — Collins has long been someone they think they should be able to beat. But the race is still neck and neck. If Maine was still top of mind, there would be a lot of finger-pointing right now among Democrats. Jackson was the pick of the left after progressives dominated the primary with the now-disgraced Graham Platner. So Jackson’s failure to launch could be taking up a lot of internet space among chatterers, and maybe it should.

“It’s weird, for sure. And it doesn’t entirely make sense,” a Democratic operative told The Washington Sun’s Al Weaver. “Troy Jackson is not a blank canvas, like early-days Platner was. He has a long governing record in the state, for better and worse, and he just seems to have not hit his stride as a statewide candidate.”

The Senate map has expanded so much for Democrats now that they’re getting excited about places like Kansas (moved yesterday to “toss up” by The Cook Political Report) and comfortable about places like North Carolina (moved to “likely Democrat”). Alaska? Sure, Democrats say. Nebraska? Trump just went there to shore up votes, what else do you need to know?? 

Democrats still have to pick up four seats to win the Senate majority, which remains a tall order. But suddenly, they’re seeing options everywhere. That means Maine may not be the must-win for the party of just a few months ago. Does this race moving to the edges of the national spotlight benefit Collins or Jackson? Let’s see how the debates play out.

More: DOJ Asks Judge to Shut Down Discovery Motion in Kennedy Center Case • Is the U.S. Prepared for Another Pandemic? • WSJ: Inside Bessent’s Treasury: Tension, Turnover and Unmet Economic Goals





FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


The GOP’s October in one quote: “Look, $4 gas, $6 diesel is unacceptable. I think we all agree on that, but it’s still not enough to vote for a communist,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer told our Reese Gorman at a campaign stop in Texas. Emmer name-checked Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico but added that the line applies to “all these other candidates that they’re putting up for office.”

Inside Republican health care messaging: Former Rep. Brad Wenstrup and Trump-aligned pollster John McLaughlin have been offering Republicans a briefing on how to talk about health care costs this cycle, The Sun’s Kadia Goba reports, and battleground ad buys show that some candidates are taking their advice. Even as public polling has found Democrats leading on the issue — by a 2-1 margin, according to KFF — Wenstrup and McLaughlin say Republicans can stay in the game by talking about waste, fraud and abuse.

In Iowa, Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and the party’s Senate nominee, Rep. Ashley Hinson, have called out “Big Insurance” on the trail. Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-New Jersey) is talking about insurance companies, too, promising to make them offer more access to mental health coverage.

“Here is the pivotal shift: Republicans have stopped playing defense,” said GOP strategist Rob Burgess. “For years our side treated health care as the other team’s turf and hoped the subject wouldn’t come up.”



FROM TEXAS


Angela Paxton wants to end Citizens United: Yes, that Angela Paxton, the one who cut a passive-aggressive ad for her estranged husband, Ken Paxton, the other day. The Sun’s Paul Kane reports on her quest to pass a constitutional amendment that would overturn the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United ruling. She views it as a states’ rights question, and belongs to part of a growing bipartisan movement. “The idea that Texas should decide for Texas, that’s all this is,” she told Paul. “It’s not saying we should have this campaign finance law or this campaign finance law.”

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


After the pocket rescissions: The Sun’s Jackie Llanos reports on two government initiatives defunded by the Trump administration last year — the High School Equivalency Program and the College Assistance Migrant Program. At the time, the White House said the Biden-era programs “laundered taxpayer dollars to radical open borders NGOs who provided legal services to illegal aliens.” But Jackie reports on the American citizens whose education plans have been thrown into chaos by the legally dubious pocket rescissions.





PODCAST

It’s the Washington Sun Cast — taped in front of a live audience! The Sun’s Igor Bobic, Kadia Goba and Paul Kane emptied their notebooks from the campaign trail to tell us what they think this year’s October surprise might be.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Biden officials say they had no warning of Oct. 7 attacks in Israel: “We were as surprised as the Israelis were,” Harrison Mann, a Defense Intelligence Agency official at the time who resigned in response to U.S. policy during the war in Gaza, told The Sun’s Akbar Shahid Ahmed in a new report that includes an excerpt from Akbar’s book “Crossing the Red Line” about the Biden White House and Gaza. Akbar details how discussions about pre-attack intelligence have spurred questions about U.S. reliance on the Israelis for intel on the region.

Recent reports say Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by Arab governments of a looming attack by Palestinians in Gaza, but did not pass the tip to his own country’s military. That tip was not communicated to the U.S. either, Akbar writes. “We rely too heavily on Israel rather than developing our own ability to get information,” said Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas), a member of the House Intelligence Committee.

More: Lawyers for Olympian Cleared in Reflecting Pool Case Demand a Watchdog Probe • Sen. Murphy Was Denied Entry to a U.S. Military Base in Qatar

  • The Inescapable Hasan Piker, by Simon van Zuylen-Wood for New York magazine

entries.title: Angela Paxton Leads the Push to Overturn Citizens United
entries.summary: The Texas state senator and other state legislators see the 2026 elections as a “tipping point” toward ending dark money.
entries.content:
Angela Paxton is not the likeliest figure to lead the movement against big spending by special interests in elections across the nation.

Paxton is a conservative state senator from Texas, whose estranged husband is benefiting from close to $200 million in unlimited, hard-to-trace spending in his Senate race. She even appeared in a super PAC ad last weekend asking Texans to “vote the ticket” and support Ken Paxton, despite what she considers his moral failings in their marriage.

But Angela Paxton came to Washington last week as part of a bipartisan delegation of state legislators preaching the gospel of barring big money in elections, particularly those undisclosed donations that might be coming from overseas or other nefarious interests.

This fall’s elections, particularly in her home state, are so overwhelmed by outside money that Paxton believes Americans are finally ready to pass a constitutional amendment that would overturn the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision that set the stage for today’s politics.

“We may be at a tipping point. I hope we are, because the fundamental issue is each state should be able to design [campaign laws] for itself. That's how the system was built. The courts have moved us away from that, and this will restore it,” Paxton told The Washington Sun in an exclusive interview.

The group of state legislators is working with American Promise, a nonprofit that is leading an underdog effortto allow states and Congress to rewrite laws regarding how political campaigns are financed.

The plan is to take an outside-in approach to changing the Constitution that would demonstrate to Capitol Hill that three-fourths of states (38) stand ready and willing to approve what would be the 28th amendment to the nation’s founding charter. The leaders of this movement want to demonstrate to Washington that the support is out there if they have the courage to move on the issue.

The concept, laid out in barely two pages of legislative text, is either incredibly naive — considering it’s been more than 50 years since this polarized nation approved a new amendment — or perfectly simple in its appeal to conservatives, centrists and liberals alike.

“I think that as a nation, collectively, we're tired right now. We're exhausted,” Republican Utah state Rep. Jason Thompson, who’s facing an onslaught of direct mail financed by out-of-state liberals in his reelection bid, told The Sun in between meetings with Utah’s delegation in the Cannon Office Building.

“We the people are tired,” he said. “We're tired of how Washington is spending money. We're tired of how money is being used to influence our votes, and I think that's what's led to a huge increase in overall frustration by both parties.”

So far, American Promise has helped organize resolutions of support in 25 state legislatures, running the ideological gamut from Utah to Vermont.

Other states are moving in that direction as well, such as Texas, where Paxton is vice chair of the committee charged with writing election law and has already introduced a bill supporting the constitutional amendment. She expects to try to move quickly once the Legislature comes back into session in January, arguing that this is a states’ rights issue at the core of the conservative movement.

“The idea that Texas should decide for Texas, that's all this is,” she told The Sun. “It's not saying we should have this campaign finance law or this campaign finance law.”

She was particularly moved by a referendum in Maine to ban foreign money in campaigns that won overwhelming support, only to be overturned last week by federal courts following precedents set by the Supreme Court.

Her message to fellow conservatives receiving big support from outside money — such as Ken Paxton and other Texas Republicans — is that they will fare better.

“Even a candidate who's getting a lot of money from a super PAC, if you put them on the spot and say, ‘Do you believe we should allow foreign money in our elections?’ No Republican is going to be able to stand on a policy like that,” she said.

Should the outside movement gather up 38 states ready to support the amendment, Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Michigan) has already written a bill to add it to the nation’s founding document.

“Free speech and competitive campaigns are essential to our democracy, but our elections should not be determined by elite megadonors,” Barrett said in introducing the measure.

But the issue hasn’t gained much traction inside Congress, as Barrett has just one co-sponsor: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif).

And for more than 15 years, the Supreme Court has been increasing the ability of big money to influence campaigns, including this year’s decision, written by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, that weakened the separation between candidates for federal office and allied party campaign committees, allowing them to coordinate expenditures they hadn’t been able to discuss before.

Kavanaugh wrote that the “fullest and most urgent” application of the First Amendment applied to the “conduct of campaigns” for public office. “Spending money on one’s own speech must be permitted,” he wrote.

That’s a view that Republicans like Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky have been pushing for 25 to 30 years, helping to create a system of super PACs taking unlimited donations that have often spent more money than parties’ actual candidates.

Democrats, after denouncing such spending, have also engaged in this political arms race and have their fair share of super PAC allies who will spend hundreds of millions of dollars this fall, albeit nothing that can match the likes of Elon Musk, who spent more than $200 million in 2024 helping Trump.

Paxton, who isn’t up for election this year, spent a relaxing few days in Washington away from the airwaves of Texas, where it’s not just the Senate and governor’s races that are dominant. State senators there represent over 1 million people — more than a member of the U.S. House — and Paxton estimates that in her first campaign, in 2018, she spent $3.5 million.

Opposition to this flood of money has gained surprising resonance in some of the most rural, conservative states like Utah and Wyoming, where once-quaint state and local elections are turning into highly financed battles resembling the uglier races for Congress.

Republican Wyoming state Rep. Andrew Byron recalled that where a campaign for a “really competitive” seat representing about 9,500 people once cost about $5,000, that same seat now “can easily go into six figures.”

The weapon of choice in these low-population states has been direct-mail pieces, not the highly produced TV ads dominating national contests.

Candidates for state legislature used to produce a few pieces each election, mostly touting their own views and critiquing their opponent. Byron estimates 100 pieces of mail flooded his home ahead of the state’s unusually competitive primary elections this summer.

“I bet 80 of those or 90 of those don't have any ties to any entity in Wyoming,” he told The Sun.

His travel companion to Washington last week, state Sen. Mike Gierau, one of two Democrats in Wyoming’s upper legislature, said these direct-mail pieces often aren’t even about local issues that the Legislature handles.

“The representative is driving illegals across the border, picking up fentanyl, and then, you know, dropping off that with the pornography at the local library,” Gierau said, mocking the extreme content. “It plays to these national hot-button issues.”

He works with Republicans out of necessity, and his argument for them to support the constitutional amendment comes down to how cheap elections are in Wyoming, relative to larger population states, and the damage that big money could do there.

“A group of people, a small group of people, can sit in their room and say, "I can turn the tide of an entire state election with less than $1 million. I can actually buy a legislature for that,” Gierau said.

In Utah, Thompson watched with horror when about $50,000 in dark money — he believes it was from liberals in the Jackson Hole region — poured into a local mayor’s race to impact the outcome. He is bracing to face up to $175,000 worth of outside super PAC money in his November election campaign.

“Which means I have to go then fundraise that much more money,” Thompson lamented.

These state lawmakers, especially the Republicans, believe that the first law they would pass, if they could, would be to mandate immediate public disclosure of big donations along with banning foreign contributions.

Paxton wants the key connection to be between candidates and voters, not candidates and donors.

“What we have is our candidates spend all their time raising money,” she said. “What we really want is them interacting with voters, so people can get to know them.”

entries.summary: Banned Books Week, author Barbara Kingsolver and the Swedish Embassy.
entries.content:
Thursday 

Beyond the Book Bans: The Samuels Public Library Story

Central Library, 1015 N. Quincy St., Arlington, 6 to 7:30 p.m., free

In honor of Banned Books Week, Arlington Public Library welcomes leaders from Samuels Public Library in Front Royal, Virginia. Last year, Warren County Board of Supervisors voted to defund the 200-year-old library, responding to residents who found some materials objectionable. Although some county funding has since been restored, the librarians will visit Arlington to discuss navigating community controversy.

“The Flying Lovers of Vitebsk” at Theater J

1529 16th St. NW, 7:30 p.m., $49

Artist Marc Chagall and his wife and model Bella are the main characters in this 2017 play with music receiving its D.C. premiere. True to the title (and imagery in Chagall’s paintings), two aerial artists will perform in the show at Theater J, Washingtonian’s theater focusing on the Jewish diaspora. Performances continue through Nov. 1.

More to explore: Bertha: Grateful Drag show at the 9:30 Club.

Friday 


Michael Kosta at The Howard Theatre

620 T St. NW, 7 p.m., $44 to $67

There aren’t too many pro tennis players who have pivoted to late-night TV, but that’s Michael Kosta’s schtick, and he is sticking to it. The 6’4” comic has been a guest on “The Tonight Show,” Conan and Seth Meyers, and since 2024 has been on the rotating list of hosts for “The Daily Show,” but he still makes time for stand-up. His “Big Dad Energy” tour draws on his varied professional experiences and personal responsibilities as the parent of two girls and a dog named Walter.

Author Barbara Kingsolver at Lisner Auditorium

730 21st St. NW, 7 p.m., $61

Bestselling author Barbara Kingsolver follows up her 2023 Pulitzer Prize winner “Demon Copperhead” with “Partita,” the story of an aspiring pianist who abandons conservatory training for farm life, far away from the lights of concert halls, until an expected reunion forces her to reprise the past. Presented in partnership with Politics and Prose.

More to explore: ’90s cover band White Ford Bronco at The Atlantis

Saturday


Family Day at the Embassy of Sweden

2900 K St. NW, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., free, registration required

You’ve taken your kid to Ikea, now take them to Family Day at the Swedish Embassy. This annual event is a considerable upgrade from the Småland ball pit. Enjoy crafts, storytime, Swedish “fika” sweets and “Tillie the Terrible Swede,” a puppet show about the pioneering Swedish bicycle racer Matilda Andersson.

Capitol Hill Porchfest 

Capitol Hill, 2 to 6 p.m., free

What if the real reason Congress took an early election recess is to avoid the first Capitol Hill Porchfest? Just a thought. One hundred and fifty-nine bands have signed up to perform on 52 porches over a four-hour period this Saturday, with music from Potomac Avenue all the way north to I Street. The festival is sponsored by Waymo, so look out for autonomous vehicles.

More to explore: The IN Series opens M.A.K.A.do, a contemporary riff on Gilbert and Sullivan, at Arena Stage.

Sunday 


Costume Swap at the SPARK! Art Market

2700 S. Nelson St., Arlington, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., free

Arlington’s monthly art market gets on the recycle/reduce/reuse bandwagon with a costume swap for revelers of all ages. Bring last year’s Minion costume and come home with everything you need to trick-or-treat as a witch. The usual roster of more than a dozen artists will be at the park selling everything from candles to ceramics while a DJ spins Halloween novelty songs and the Rossana “Mobile Espresso Experience” pumps out the lattes.

“Oedipus in Seattle” at Studio 1469

 1469 Harvard St. NW, 7 p.m., $20

Three pairs of respected DMV actors will take turns portraying Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks in this parody of “Sleepless in Seattle,” but with three caveats: There are no rehearsals, they’ll be receiving stage directions via headphones, and the rom-com’s plot will be mashed up with Sophocles’ incestual tragedy “Oedipus Rex.” (Also Saturday night; Monday show sold-out.)

More to explore: The documentary “If You Lived Here You Would Be Home Now” screens at the National Gallery.

entries.title: Republicans Want to Flip the Script on Health Care
entries.summary: Polling finds public trust swinging hard toward Democrats on controlling costs, but some GOP candidates see an opening.
entries.content:
Back in the summer, physician and former Republican Rep. Brad Wenstrup and Trump-aligned pollster John McLaughlin offered coaching to House Republicans on how to talk about health care: Lean in.

Republican strategists say the party has treated the topic as Democratic turf for years, and such advice may sound counterintuitive a year after Republicans passed $1 trillion in federal health care budget cuts.

But some GOP lawmakers are taking it, running ads on targeted health care subjects in swing districts in states like Iowa, New York and New Jersey, where candidates and strategists recognize they need an affirmative response — especially as open-enrollment season opens this month for millions of Americans.

Wenstrup and McLaughlin explained why in briefings to the National Republican Congressional Committee and the Republican Study Committee that offered polling data that pegged health insurance costs as voters’ leading health care concern.

The data also suggested ways to push back. One McLaughlin & Associates survey of 2,000 likely voters commissioned by Americans for Health Excellence, which Wenstrup leads, said 65% of voters were more likely to vote for a Republican candidate who supports cracking down on fraud, waste and abuse by insurance companies.

“Our polling shows common-sense pocketbook solutions have support from more than eight in ten voters, including strong majorities of Republicans, Democrats and Independents,” Wenstrup said in a statement to The Washington Sun. “That is not just good policy. It is winning ground for candidates and smart to work on behalf of patients.”

While campaigns are likely making their own decisions, such ideas are being promoted in competitive districts.

Rep. Mike Lawler of New York has highlighted affordability in his ads. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa pledged to take on “Big Insurance” companies, as did Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate. Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey has focused on ensuring patients have equal access to physical and mental health care through their insurance coverage.

For Republicans in competitive districts, campaigning on health care offers an opportunity to reach beyond their usual voters, said Kristin Davison, a national Republican consultant at Axiom Strategies.

“It's also something that gives a permission slip to someone that's not used to voting Republican to consider you because you're talking about an issue that Republicans haven't necessarily dominated in the past,” Davison said.

Rob Burgess, CEO of Connector, Inc. and a national Republican strategist, described the shift as Republicans becoming more willing to compete on the issue.

“Here is the pivotal shift: Republicans have stopped playing defense,” Burgess said. “For years our side treated health care as the other team's turf and hoped the subject wouldn't come up.”

Burgess argued that the pressure starts with candidates hearing about affordability in their districts.

“Those members aren't following a memo. They're following their voters, and the party is catching up to what they already know,” he said.

Sarah Chamberlain, the president of the Republican Main Street Partnership, also said the new messaging on health care is not a broader Republican strategy but reflects more of a district-by-district approach. She pointed to Kean, who has publicly discussed his own mental health struggles, as an example of a candidate whose personal experience shapes his health care priorities.

Lawler, who has long discussed health care, told The Sun in an interview that he helped block proposals to reduce the federal government’s share of Medicaid funding and negotiated an extension of New York’s tax on managed care organizations, which he said preserved $1.2 billion for the state’s hospital system.

Lawler was also one of four Republicans who signed a discharge petition to force a vote to extend enhanced Affordable Care Act marketplace insurance subsidies for three years. The bill passed the House but ultimately stalled in the Senate.

Such efforts and ads, however, are running into some on-the-ground reality that millions of Americans are about to encounter as the annual process of updating insurance choices starts later this month.

Open enrollment for Medicare recipients starts Oct. 15. Shopping for ACA health plans in the federal marketplace begins Nov. 1, and an analysis by the health care research organization KFF found those shoppers will face median proposed premium increases of 15%. Many people who get insurance through work will also start seeing in October and November how much more will come out of their paychecks next year.

And while the GOP polling may have identified some winning messages, a new KFF survey released Tuesday suggests voters are not really absorbing them. The poll of more than 1,000 Americans found Democrats holding a 42% to 22% edge over Republicans for which party they trust more to handle health care costs. That is a dramatic jump since April, when Democrats had a 37% to 26% lead.

Liz Hamel of KFF told The Sun that Republican messaging on fraud, waste and abuse has resonated with voters but doesn’t necessarily translate to a belief that prioritizing fraud will lower their costs.

She added that Republicans’ historical advantage on the economy had sometimes extended to health, even as voters favored Democrats on programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. But that has recently changed.

“We're finding that Democrats even have an edge on health care costs among voters,” she said.

Whether Republicans can turn their health care pitches into greater voter trust remains an open question, even if there is not much time left before the midterm elections. Burgess said that trust ultimately depends on results.

“Parties do own issues, but ownership isn't a deed. It's a lease, and it renews on performance,” he said.

entries.title: Trump Says He’s Reviewing Top Advisers’ Work for Far-Right Balkan Government
entries.summary: “If there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday he was looking into reports that two of his top political advisers had performed consulting work for a pro-Russian nationalist government in Bosnia-Herzegovina, suggesting that he may fire both longtime confidants if there is a conflict of interest.

The comments followed a bombshell report in The New York Times that Chris LaCivita and James Blair traveled to Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, shortly before its elections on Sunday to advise the government on voting-related matters. Each was paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the work, the Times reported.

Trump defended the arrangement in a post on Truth Social, saying both men are outside consultants and are allowed to work for other clients.

“They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients,” he said, adding that he planned to ask them for an accounting of their client list.

“If there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump added.

The president later addressed the situation during a press conference in the Oval Office, insisting that there was likely no conflict of interest because they do not work directly in the White House. 

“They're not sitting around a Cabinet table or anything like that,” he said, adding: “I'm sure they have many clients, but that would be true with everybody in Washington.”

Both men hold prominent roles in Trump’s political operation ahead of next month’s midterm elections. LaCivita co-managed Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, while Blair served as his political director and later as a White House deputy chief of staff. Blair has since taken a leading role in executing Trump’s midterm strategy.

Republika Srpska is governed by the nationalist SNSD, the party of longtime Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik, who has maintained close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Trump administration lifted U.S. sanctions on Dodik, his family members and several allies in October 2025.

entries.title: Rubio’s State Department Pushes Russia for More Info on Lab Worker’s Death
entries.summary: It warned Moscow that withholding details on a potential infectious disease was a failure to comply with international agreements.
entries.content:
U.S. officials warned Russia that it was failing to comply with global health obligations by not sharing details about the death of a plague researcher in Siberia. The pressure from the Americans came in the form of a confidential diplomatic communication, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.

Following the death of 28-year-old lab worker Daria Shipilova, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for Moscow to release more details about what made her sick.

“We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that we can react accordingly and appropriately,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday. “But we're gonna have to make those decisions on the basis of the information that we're learning and being provided, and so far that is still quite limited.”

The mysterious circumstances around the death has prompted Russian officials to quarantine a reported 200 people.

President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin “soon.”

The secrecy surrounding the potential infectious disease is the latest sore spot between the U.S. and Russia. Trump had said he’d negotiate an end to Putin’s war in Ukraine on the first day of his second term. Two years later, the fighting appears no closer to resolution. And while the president signed into law a sweeping Russia sanctions bill last month, his administration also faced backlash for inviting Putin to the G20 summit in Miami later this year.

“We haven't ended Russia-Ukraine yet," Trump said at a Tuesday event in Baltimore. “I'm working on that one, that one I thought would be the easiest one for me. But … that's going to happen too pretty soon.”

When asked for comment, representatives for the White House and State Department referred The Washington Sun to Trump and Rubio’s comments.

A 2005 global health pact called the International Health Regulations requires countries that experience an event that could become an international public health emergency to notify the World Health Organization within 24 hours, provide updates and share lab results.

While Moscow has provided some information to WHO, The Wall Street Journal reported, it hasn’t provided detailed answers required by the agreement.

Russian authorities said Shipilova, who worked at Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died suddenly of pneumonia earlier this month. With gaps in the information coming out of Russia, some public health officials worry her illness could have been caused by a deadly pathogen present in her lab work.

Russia has denied those claims.

Russia’s national public health agency told Russian media on Monday that after a comprehensive analysis of Shipilova’s body, they found “no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities.” It added in a separate statement to the Russian News Agency that evidence of COVID-19 and a cold virus had been found among the people being quarantined.

The WHO has stated there’s a low risk that the disease that killed the lab worker would spread globally. Trump ordered the U.S. to withdraw from the international health organization upon his return to the White House, citing what he called the organization’s “mishandling” of the pandemic that began during his first term.

The U.S. Embassy in Russia on Tuesday warned Americans in the country of the increased health risk and said the American government would have limited ability to help citizens there.

entries.title: Hillary Clinton Endorses Her First Candidate of 2026
entries.summary: The former first lady and secretary of state endorsed Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in her run for U.S. Senate.
entries.content:
Hillary Clinton endorsed her first candidate of the 2026 election cycle this week.

The former first lady and secretary of state endorsed Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, in her Senate run against Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter and commentator.

Clinton announced the endorsement on Tuesday, her first midterm endorsement for a House or Senate candidate.

“Peggy Flanagan has spent her career fighting for children and families, from the Children's Defense Fund to the Lieutenant Governor's office, and she's delivered for them,” Clinton said in a statement. “I know she'll be that same champion in the Senate, and I’m proud to endorse her.”

Clinton also criticized President Donald Trump amid rising prices.

"Donald Trump has made it harder for families to afford childcare, groceries, and health care for their kids. His tariffs and war in Iran are driving up prices, and his budget ripped health care and food assistance away from children so billionaires could get another tax cut,” she said.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a statement, Flanagan said she was “honored” to have Clinton’s endorsement.

“Secretary Clinton has spent five decades fighting for those families, and I'm honored to have her support as we take that fight to the United States Senate,” Flanagan wrote.

Several high-profile politicians have endorsed Flanagan, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar.

Clinton began her career at the Children's Defense Fund, where she worked as a staff attorney and chaired the organization’s board. Between 2001 and 2009, she served as a U.S. senator for New York, and she ran for president in 2008 and 2016.

Flanagan previously served as the head of Children’s Defense Fund in Minnesota, where she co-chaired a campaign to raise the minimum wage and index it to inflation.

“Long before she was First Lady, Senator, or Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton was knocking on doors for the Children's Defense Fund, making the case that every child in this country deserves a fair shot. That same work shaped me,” Flanagan said in her statement.

entries.title: Trump Wants a New Camp David at His West Palm Beach Golf Club
entries.summary: Under a new plan, part of the county-owned property would be provided to the federal government, while the rest would remain a private golf course.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump wants to build a permanent Camp David-style presidential retreat at his golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida, according to a letter a lawyer for the property sent last month to local officials.

And the county is seriously considering his proposal, County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo told The Washington Post. He said officials are in contact with the General Services Administration and have begun plans to identify a parcel for the project.

Palm Beach County owns the land beneath Trump International Golf Club West Palm Beach and leases it to Trump's company, the Trump Organization.

Under the terms listed in the letter, the Trump Organization would continue operating the course next to the presidential compound and keep making lease payments to the county. Representatives for Trump told county officials last week that the government-owned retreat would have a separate entrance from the private club.

No final agreement with the federal government has been announced.

The Palm Beach Post first reported the proposal last month after Harvey Oyer, a lawyer representing Trump International Golf Club, sent a letter to county commissioners outlining plans for a permanent presidential golf course. The newspaper later reported that county staff had begun exploring the proposal.

Under the plan, part of the county-owned property would be provided to the federal government for a presidential residence and related facilities, while the rest would remain a private golf course. Oyer said Trump would pay to build the presidential facilities.

The site could host future presidents, foreign leaders and international summits. Future presidents would also receive complimentary memberships to the Trump-owned club.

“Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County,” Oyer wrote to county commissioners last month.

Oyer said construction would not be completed before Trump leaves office and called the project “a gift” to Trump’s successors.

“My understanding is that President Trump views this as a lasting contribution to the presidency and to those who will hold the office after him,” Abruzzo told the Post.

A White House official told the Post that the property offered several advantages for presidential use, including its proximity to an airport and law enforcement, existing security features and the lack of homes and large buildings immediately surrounding the course.

Trump reported $36.9 million in earnings from the West Palm Beach club in his most recent financial disclosure.

The Florida retreat would not replace Camp David. Presidents have used the government-owned Maryland compound for decades as a getaway from Washington and a venue for meetings with foreign leaders.

Trump has generally chosen his own properties when spending time away from Washington. He has also been dismissive of the Maryland retreat in the past, once saying its appeal would wear off after about half an hour.

Another Trump-owned club in Palm Beach, Mar-a-Lago, was once intended for a similar purpose. Marjorie Merriweather Post arranged for the estate to become a federal presidential retreat, but the government later returned it to the Post Foundation following her death. Trump bought the property in 1985.
