entries.title: U.S. Military Bans Booze for Soldiers in Okinawa After a Marine Was Accused of Murder
entries.summary: Also included in the order was a 48-hour pause on operations and mandatory discussions on off-duty behavior and Okinawan culture.
entries.content:
The U.S. military is instituting a 48-hour alcohol ban for soldiers stationed in Okinawa after a Marine was accused of murdering a 39-year-old Japanese woman, setting off an international incident that has inflamed tensions between the two countries.

The “Period of Training,” as military leaders called it, will run from Wednesday to Friday. Also included in the order was a 48-hour pause on operations and mandatory discussions on off-duty behavior, enforcement mechanisms, alcohol awareness, Okinawan culture and alliance responsibilities, according to a memo written by Lt. Gen. Benjamin T. Watson, the Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and posted to social media Tuesday evening.

The alcohol restriction applies to private residences, Watson noted. Bases will remain open for mission-essential and essential personal movement, according to an FAQ page.

Watson said the opportunity would allow military officials to train service members on standards, discipline and responsibilities as “members of the Okinawan community.”

“Every member of this force must understand that individual conduct has consequences,” wrote Watson.

Following the training, service members will enter a 30-day “Period of Reflection.” During that time, the military will implement restrictions on service members to remind them that “liberty is a privilege and a collective responsibility.”

Additionally, service members must follow a midnight curfew and are required to be back on base in their assigned quarters or off-base housing from midnight to 5 a.m., the memo states.

The military will also implement enhanced supervision at gates across all installations on Okinawa. Officials have not released details on what the enhanced security measures would entail.

A review of liberty policies and procedures will also be conducted, and recommendations will be shared with the Okinawa Area Coordinating Committee for potential implementation.

It’s unclear if alcohol consumption will be allowed during the reflection period.

In response to a question about why force-wide measures are being directed, the U.S. military said: “Incidents of this nature demand a pause for reflection. Every interaction with the people of Okinawa either builds or undermines the trust essential to our alliance.”

Officials arrested 20-year-old Devin Jacob Ballard on Sunday in connection with the murder of Anna Yagi. Okinawa police believe Ballard strangled Yagi in a Naha hotel room Saturday and stole her personal items, The Associated Press reported.

Ballard, who was based at Futenma Air Station, has denied the allegations, local outlets reported.

Okinawa is home to 32 U.S. Military bases. The U.S. has maintained an active military presence in the region since 1945. More than 50,000 American troops are stationed in Japan under a bilateral security agreement, according to The Associated Press.

The ongoing military presence in Okinawa has been a long-standing source of frustration for the local community, the AP reported. About 70% of the U.S. military’s presence in Japan is concentrated on the island.

However, some residents view it as a valuable asset in response to ongoing threats from China, according to the outlet.

The murder has nonetheless raised new questions about the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, with local leaders taking aim at the two countries’ security agreements.

On Wednesday, Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters, “The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” according to a translation published by the AP.

“It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged,” he added.

entries.title: Ken Paxton Audio Keeps Leaking: Now It's His Frustrations Over Iran
entries.summary: Audio of the private admission was reported just before Paxton is expected to appear with President Donald Trump at a San Antonio rally.
entries.content:
Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, told donors and lobbyists he believes the war in Iran and high gas prices have hurt his campaign.

His comments, in which he said he doesn’t “know what’s behind some of the decisions,” were made in a private gathering held in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24 and reported by Axios on Wednesday. It’s the third leak that’s emerged from the fundraiser, drawing scrutiny to the candidate in a race that is increasingly seen as promising for Democrats.

“So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable,” Paxton can be heard saying in the latest clip, adding that affordability is “by far our biggest problem.”

“It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” Paxton said. “When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel … people are feeling the pinch.”

The latest report was published ahead of a campaign rally on Wednesday in San Antonio, where Paxton is expected to appear alongside President Donald Trump.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, Madison Cercy, a campaign spokesperson for Paxton, said that the audio is a “non-story.”

“The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store," Cercy said. "President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families' pockets."

In other clips from the September meeting, obtained by The New York Times and Politico, Paxton told donors that his polling numbers were hurt by the GOP midterm convention hosted in Dallas last month and said his campaign’s direction was driven by establishment figures.

“I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming, you know, from D.C.,” Paxton said in the audio obtained by Politico earlier this week. “I don’t control the message or what we’re doing.”

James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in the Texas Senate race, briefly responded to Paxton’s remark on social media.

“Ken Paxton is a puppet,” Talarico said.

On Tuesday, Trump told reporters he hadn’t heard Paxton’s comments.

“Ken and everyone is doing much better now that I’ve started the rallies,” Trump said. “It’s brought a whole new awareness to how great the economy is doing.”

The topic of affordability has created a rift between Trump and some Republicans ahead of the November midterms. The president has repeatedly referred to concerns over inflation and prices as a “hoax,” but voters across the country have signaled that economic issues are top of mind.

When speaking with donors, Paxton suggested that one of his campaign proposals, which includes write-offs for housing, health care and family-related expenses, is one way he would address the issue.

"I'm just trying to figure out ways I can help people,” he said. “That's the only way: I can propose legislation.”
entries.author: Emma Ruby

entries.title: DNC Sues Trump Administration, Alleging Taxpayer-Funded Ads Violate Propaganda Law
entries.summary: The complaint alleges that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda and accuses Trump of personally directing them.
entries.content:
By Ali Swenson

The Democratic National Committee on Wednesday sued President Donald Trump’s administration for recent television advertisements that promoted his political message while costing taxpayers millions of dollars.

The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda and accuses Trump of personally directing them. It asks the court to declare the ads illegal and stop the use of federal funds to pay for them.

Trump has faced bipartisan backlash for the ads, which glorify him and echo his campaign pitch as voters cast early ballots with the midterm elections less than a month away.

The spots, which began airing in September, already have cost more than $12 million to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, and a total of $20 million in Homeland Security Department funding has been tapped to pay for them.

Responding Monday to the criticism, Trump defended the ads as “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” but said he’d pay for them using his MAGA Inc. super PAC going forward.

But on Tuesday, the fifth ad in the campaign began airing with the notice “paid for by the U.S. Government,” promoting Trump’s military actions in Venezuela earlier this year. The same day, Trump made it clear he hasn’t committed to reimbursing any money that has already been spent, telling reporters “we’ll decide.”

DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement that Trump is misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November.”

“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes," he added.

Legal experts have suggested the ads run afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda,” and potentially other federal laws. The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175 million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. Legal experts have said the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs.

The defendants in the lawsuit — Trump, the White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget — didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: White House Social Media Guru Earned at Least $1 Million From a Trump Media Investment
entries.summary: Deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino reported seven-figure capital gains from stock in the company behind Truth Social.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s longtime White House social media guru scored a seven-figure payday last year from the president’s social media company, according to a new federal financial disclosure.

White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino disclosed earning between $1 million and $5 million in capital gains during 2025 from a stock holding in Trump Media & Technology Group. The company runs the Truth Social platform that the president regularly uses to announce government decisions, debate national affairs, promote his friends and lambaste his enemies.

Scavino valued his Trump Media & Technology Group stock holding at between $1 million and $5 million, according to his financial disclosure, which he filed last month and the federal Office of Government Ethics released this week. (Government officials are only required by law to disclose stock values in broad ranges.)

Scavino joins recently departed White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt among White House officials who personally invested last year in a Trump business venture.

Scavino previously directed White House social media efforts. He has continued to play a key role managing Trump’s social media presence, as The Washington Post reported last year, while personally profiting from his stake in Trump’s social media outfit.

Scavino purchased his Trump Media & Technology Group stock prior to joining Trump’s second presidential administration and becoming a government employee, a White House official said Tuesday.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, White House counsel Will Scharf said his office “regularly works with appointees to provide ethics guidance and help ensure compliance with applicable federal ethics laws and regulations. In this case, we believe Dan Scavino complied with those requirements and have no further concerns.”

Office of Government Ethics official Scott F. Gast certified Scavino’s personal financial disclosure, which federal law requires for high-ranking executive branch employees, as “in compliance with applicable laws and regulations.” Another agency official, Megan Granahan, concurred on Oct. 1, according to Scavino’s disclosure document.

Office of Government Ethics spokesperson Patrick Shepherd declined to comment, saying that while his agency is “committed to transparency and citizen oversight of government,” it “does not respond to questions about specific individuals.”

Aaron Scherb, a longtime federal government ethics watchdog, suggested Scavino could avoid overstepping any ethical lines by divesting his Trump Media stock, placing his assets in a qualified blind trust or shifting his wealth into diversified financial instruments such as mutual funds.

Scavino reported having between $850,000 and $1.75 million in Vanguard exchange-traded funds and $500,000 to $1 million in a bank account.

Scavino’s financial disclosure also indicates that he earned up to $100,000 in capital gains from stock in financial platform company Robinhood Markets, which he valued at between $100,000 and $250,000.

Robinhood has partnered with the U.S. Treasury to serve as broker for Trump Accounts, a tax-advantaged government investment account designed to help American children build wealth. The company also contributed $2 million to Trump’s 2025 presidential inauguration. Its stock price is up more than 100% from when Trump began his second term.

Scavino has previously drawn legal scrutiny for his actions while serving in the White House.

In 2017, the Office of Special Counsel ruled that Scavino violated the Hatch Act by calling for the defeat of then-Rep. Justin Amash (R-Michigan). He received a warning letter.

The Department of Justice also declined to file contempt of Congress charges against Scavino in 2022 after he refused to honor a subpoena issued by the U.S. House select committee investigating the January 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.
entries.author: Dave Levinthal

entries.title: Hegseth Tells USS Abraham Lincoln Sailors ‘the Media’ Overstated Their Problems
entries.summary: The comments came after months of reports detailing declining morale, supply problems and mental health struggles during the aircraft carrier’s record-setting deployment.
entries.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth greeted thousands of U.S. Navy sailors returning to the U.S. mainland Wednesday from a record-setting deployment aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, telling the crew in prepared remarks that media reports had overstated problems aboard the carrier while simultaneously acknowledging their achievements.

Hegseth presented the carrier strike group with the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest decoration given collectively to a U.S. military unit.

The citation said the group flew 3,693 combat sorties, launched 450 Tomahawk missiles and sank 64 Iranian warships during its deployment — which he denied was plagued by dysfunction or low morale.

“There were a few folks in the media who tried to turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale, or a symbol of a failed mission,” Hegseth told the crew as the carrier returned to San Diego.

“When I talk to your leadership, and I have had a chance to talk to a number of you, I know it’s the exact opposite,” he said.

The comments came after months of reports of declining morale, supply problems and mental health struggles aboard the Lincoln during its unusually long deployment. The Navy has since acknowledged some resupply problems.

Hegseth previously said that reports about conditions aboard the carrier had been “completely misrepresented.”

The Navy later confirmed that eight sailors across the Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during the deployment. The figure includes sailors assigned to the carrier, its air wing, accompanying destroyers and other elements of the strike group. No sailors died by suicide.

Hegseth did not mention the suicide attempts Wednesday, though he did acknowledge the length of the deployment, noting that the crew went 265 consecutive days without a port call and had its time at sea extended twice.

The Lincoln left San Diego in November and was diverted to the Middle East in January, where it spent nearly seven months supporting U.S. operations against Iran. The deployment stretched well beyond the six-to-nine months typical for Navy ships.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: EPA Plans to Roll Back Emissions Regulations for Oil and Gas Companies
entries.summary: The Trump administration is “days not weeks” away from undoing Biden-era methane gas standards.
entries.content:
The Environmental Protection Agency plans to roll back regulations on methane emissions and other greenhouse gases for the oil and gas industry, the agency’s administrator, Lee Zeldin, announced at a meeting of the New Mexico Oil and Gas Association on Wednesday.

Zeldin told event attendees that the EPA’s program that allows third parties to identify and report large methane leaks was unnecessary and ineffective, according to reporting from the Santa Fe New Mexican.

The Biden administration adopted standards for the oil and gas industry in 2024 to reduce emissions of methane, which is more than 28 times as potent as carbon dioxide. The Trump administration suspended the implementation of the Biden administration’s standards in 2025.

In a press release, the EPA said the agency is “days not weeks away” from announcing a proposal to reconsider those standards. Zeldin said the agency had heard from energy producers that the standards were unworkable and holding back progress.

Among other changes, the reconsideration is expected to include changes to how oil wells are categorized and a rescission of the “super emitter” program that strengthened reporting on methane emissions, according to the EPA’s press release.

Mahyar Sorour, director of the Sierra Club’s Beyond Fossil Fuels Policy program, called the move “foolsish and short-sighted.”

“It took many years and carefully considered input from health experts, community advocates, and even the oil and gas industry itself to craft the achievable, common-sense methane standards,” she said in a statement. “Yet, the Trump administration, with pockets lined by the biggest polluters, has unceremoniously worked to roll back this and other standards meant to protect our health and safety.”
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Congress’ Watchdog Finds Trump Illegally Withheld More Than $1 Billion in Federal Funds
entries.summary: The White House impounded funds from the EPA and HHS last year, the Government Accountability Office reports.
entries.content:
Congress’s watchdog arm has found that the Trump administration illegally withheld federal funds last year from federal government programs at the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Health and Human Services.

In 2025, the Trump administration prevented the two agencies from distributing more than $1 billion appropriated by Congress, in prohibitions known as impoundments, according to two decisions that the Government Accountability Office sent to Congress on Wednesday.

Impoundments are illegal under a law passed in the aftermath of the Watergate scandal that further institutionalized the separation of powers. The GAO, as an arm of Congress, is the group empowered both to investigate possible impoundments and sue the executive branch over violations, but the GAO has never actually filed such a suit.

The watchdog arm is currently without an appointed or confirmed leader, and its acting general counsel is hesitant to pursue legal action, The Washington Sun previously reported. The GAO concluded in September that the Trump administration’s “pocket rescissions” of roughly $800 million in federal spending violated impoundment laws. The watchdog has previously reached impoundment decisions for several other government programs that lost funds last year.

But GAO has taken no action in response to any of those conclusions.

At the EPA, the GAO found that the agency impounded funds in 2025 when it terminated more than $1 billion worth of grants distributed under the “Community Change Grants Program,” which was created in the Inflation Reduction Act to fund climate resilience and pollution reduction efforts in disadvantaged communities.

While Congress later voted to rescind the funds once they were clawed back from the communities that won the awards, the GAO found that the initial termination and removal of funds was an impoundment.

The Office of Management and Budget did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The GAO also found HHS impounded funds when it terminated grants at the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, which investigates the nuts and bolts of how health care in the United States works.

The agency had disbursed less than 60% of its fiscal 2025 year funds, with more than $78 million unawarded, GAO found.

Over the summer, AHRQ notified recipients of more than 150 grants across 32 states that their awards had been terminated, according to a tally by Academy Health, a nonpartisan organization that advances evidence-based health policy.

Multiple AHRQ grantees received the same rationale for the cuts. Letters to grantees said the agency has new priorities, including several — nutrition, autism and “overmedicalization of children” — that are favorites of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“HHS has failed to detail to the Committee exactly how it has spent down AHRQ funding for fiscal year 2026,” said Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington), the ranking member on the Senate Appropriations Committee, in a statement.

"GAO's conclusion is clear,” said Academy Health President Aaron Carroll. “The law was not followed, and health research that Congress paid for did not happen. That should concern anyone who cares about whether our health care system actually works.”

Murray said previously that AHRQ has said it plans to fund just 90 grants this year — instead of the hundreds it typically funds — and transfer some of its dollars to other agencies.

She and Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) wrote to HHS last month asking for an explanation of how AHRQ has justified its changes.

“It is increasingly clear that once again, your department intends to ignore the law and—through a combination of gross negligence and intentional sabotage—will refuse to spend millions of taxpayer dollars that should be funding research to lower costs in the health care system and protect patients’ safety,” they wrote in the letter.
entries.author: Anna Kramer, Paige Winfield Cunningham

entries.title: FCC Considers Allowing More Political Robocalls Before Midterms, Even AI-Created Ones
entries.summary: The Republican-led FCC advanced the request for public comment and could rule on it as soon as late October.
entries.content:
By Ali Swenson

The Federal Communications Commission is considering a request by a conservative group to loosen rules on political robocalls, including those with artificial intelligence-generated voices, before November’s midterm elections.

Federal law currently bans most robocalls to cellphones unless the caller gets consent beforehand. The petition calls for a waiver that would allow political groups to use artificial or prerecorded voices in unsolicited wireless calls.

The Republican-led FCC advanced the request for public comment and could rule on it as soon as late October.

Consumer advocacy groups warn the proposed change could trigger a surge of unwanted, partisan and potentially misleading automated calls in the critical final days of the election, which will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.

The potential perils became evident two years ago during the presidential primary season when thousands of voters in New Hampshire received a robocall with an AI-generated voice of then-President Joe Biden. The call suggested voters should forgo casting a ballot in the primary and “save” their votes for the general election.

Under the waiver request before the FCC, some state and federal laws protecting against deception and voter intimidation would continue to prohibit certain misleading election-related messages. But granting it could weaken a major deterrent for bad actors, said Tim Harper, who leads the elections team at the Washington-based Center for Democracy and Technology.

Such a ruling close to Election Day would open “a huge opportunity for abuse during a period where harm has outsized impact,” he said. “Campaigns will use this technology to target voters in deceptive ways.”

The Club for Growth, a right-leaning economic policy group seeking the change, said it could help political organizations better communicate with potential voters, including in more languages, and improve polling accuracy by helping groups reach more voters. It calls current federal rules outdated and argues they dampen freedom of speech.

The nation’s communications regulatory body would have to act within a compressed schedule to grant the waiver in time to affect the midterm elections. Critics said it wouldn’t be the first time the FCC, which has become closely aligned with the president during his second term, has bypassed procedural norms to serve its political agenda.

Its Republican chairman, Brendan Carr, launched an unusual early review of broadcast licenses for several ABC-owned local broadcast stations, prompting the company to sue. It said the review years ahead of schedule was unconstitutional, a violation of free speech and a retaliation for content Trump dislikes.

The FCC didn’t respond to a request for comment on the petition.

Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat among the FCC’s three active commissioners, told The Associated Press she opposes the move and thinks it would create “a tsunami of robocalls and misinformation.”

“We’ve already seen dark money groups use AI to put candidates’ likeness behind inflammatory comments ahead of this election,” Gomez said. “Exempting political calls from the need for consumer consent would supercharge that strategy, and misleading messages could land directly on the handheld phone of nearly every voter in our country.”

In past elections, deceptive political robocalls have resulted in significant fines associated with the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, the federal law at the center of the petition.

In 2020, tens of thousands of prospective voters in majority-Black areas of the U.S. received robocalls falsely warning that if they voted by mail, they could face arrest and debt collection.

The two conservative hoaxers behind the calls, Jacob Wohl and Jack Burkman, were criminally charged for the calls and fined some $5.1 million for violating the act.

The political consultant behind the 2024 New Hampshire robocalls mimicking Biden's voice said he did it to send a wake-up call about the potential dangers of AI. He was acquitted of criminal voter suppression charges but faced fines and civil damages associated with federal law.

Shortly after the New Hampshire robocall caught authorities' attention, the FCC ruled that robocalls made with AI voice-cloning tools were outlawed under the consumer protection act.

If the commission pivots to grant the Club for Growth’s petition, political groups of all stripes could amp up their use of AI to prerecord messages that play when voters pick up the phone. They also could use the technology to engage in live conversations with voters driven by AI large language models.

Mekela Panditharatne, senior counsel in the democracy program at the Brennan Center for Justice, warned that such conversations hold risks. An AI system could make false promises about a candidate or manipulate voters in conversation by providing inaccurate or incomplete information.

Harper, from the Center for Democracy and Technology, said there also could be a privacy risk for voters who might not know how an AI agent on the line with them is capturing or repurposing their data.

The Club for Growth has argued the waiver would help create a more uniform regulatory landscape, given that unsolicited automated calls to landlines are already allowed. If the waiver is granted, callers would still be limited by certain conditions, including allowing consumers to opt out and making no more than three calls within 30 days to each individual recipient.

A public comment reply period on the petition ends Oct. 19, at which point the FCC could move forward on a decision.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Aramark Settles $4.5M Class-Action Lawsuit Over ‘Junk Fees’ at Capital One Arena
entries.summary: Customers who purchased from Aramark vendors in the arena from Oct. 1, 2024, to Dec. 31, 2025, could be entitled to compensation.
entries.content:
If you bought concessions at Capital One Arena last year, you could be entitled to a share of a $4.5 million settlement over a tucked-away “venue fee.”

The settlement stems from a lawsuit filed last November accusing Aramark, which manages most of the arena’s restaurants, of “systematically cheating” customers by charging a 3% venue fee not displayed on menus, in violation of D.C.’s consumer protection laws. The lawsuit was filed by Travelers United, a nonprofit consumer advocacy group based in the District.

“Travelers United brought this case because consumers should know the real price of what they are buying,” Lauren Wolfe, Travelers United lead counsel, told The Washington Sun. “Travelers United does not believe consumers should be subject to hidden fees.”

Photos presented in the lawsuit showed that customers could see details about the fee during the concessions check-out process only if they clicked a small information button. The resulting pop-up said the fee was added to all transactions for “ongoing maintenance and administrative costs” and that it was “not a tip or gratuity, and no portion of the venue fee is distributed to the team members serving our guests."

Aramark denied any wrongdoing and settled the class action in order to avoid ongoing litigation costs, distractions from daily business operations and the uncertainty of litigation, according to the settlement.

Customers who purchased food or beverages from Aramark-operated vendors at the arena between Oct. 1, 2024, and Dec. 31, 2025, could be entitled to compensation and can file a claim online. The deadline to file a claim is Dec. 4.

Monumental Sports & Entertainment, which owns and operates the arena, declined to comment on the settlement and its terms specifically, as it was not a party in the lawsuit.

“Providing a great experience for every guest at Capital One Arena remains our top priority, and we will continue working closely with all of our partners to ensure our guests receive the highest level of service,” a Monumental spokesperson told The Sun.

Monumental Sports & Entertainment, which owns and operates the arena, didn’t respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: D.C. Water Says Potomac River Sewage Spill Left No Lasting Impact
entries.summary: A busted pipe spilled 243 million gallons of waste into the Potomac River in January.
entries.content:
D.C. Water says there has been no lasting harm to the Potomac River after a catastrophic sewage spill in January poured 243 million gallons of untreated waste into the water.

The spill, caused by the collapse of a sewage pipe that carries wastewater from Maryland and Virginia to a treatment plant in the District, resulted in dangerous levels of E. coli bacteria in the river for months, according to daily testing performed by D.C. Water. Levels mostly evened out in March, but more robust testing started in August to get a better picture of the river’s health.

Results from those tests, which measured levels of oxygen, nutrients and metals in the river, placed each within normal range and “found no current signs of harm from the overflow,” according to an update from D.C. Water on Wednesday.

Emergency repairs restored flow to the busted section of pipe in March, but work continues on a larger project to rehabilitate the 54-mile sewer line. Following the collapse, D.C. Water identified four other sections of the pipe that required critical repairs to address “serious damage,” such as corrosion, worn concrete and exposed steel supports.

The agency had completed two of those projects as of Sept. 3. John Lisle, a D.C. Water spokesperson, said work at the other two sites is ongoing, and the agency anticipates most of the remaining projects to be finished this fall.

The Justice Department and Maryland’s Department of Environment sued D.C. Water in April for failing to properly maintain the sewer line. The Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission, a Maryland utility company that supplies water to 1.9 million residents, joined the lawsuit in September. Legal proceedings are ongoing.
entries.author: Kendall Staton

entries.title: The Trump Administration Is Looking Into Farmers’ Antitrust Concerns
entries.summary: The new inquiry into farm equipment is the latest move to reach out to rural voters ahead of the midterm elections.
entries.content:
The Federal Trade Commission and the Agriculture Department on Wednesday opened a joint public inquiry into competition in the farm equipment market, asking farmers and repair shops to document what barriers they face in getting equipment and keeping it running.

The request for information responds to a growing number of complaints USDA has received from farmers about obstacles to buying equipment and getting it serviced, according to the FTC. It covers manufacturing and distribution, including potential anticompetitive conduct.

“Everyday I hear from farmers and far too often they bring up the restrictions they face in being able to repair their own equipment,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said on X. “Added costs and lost labor time are the result of these misguided restrictions for our farmers and ranchers.”

FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson said in a social media post that the agency especially wants to hear from “independent repair providers, farmers, or manufacturing industry insiders willing to describe their firsthand experiences or provide documents. The concerns of America’s farmers deserve to be heard.”

The Trump administration has been active in recent weeks in reaching out to farmers, as high input prices stemmed from the war in Iran and a reignited trade war with Canada, a major trade partner in American agriculture.

Republicans have been forced to invest in unexpected races, with a Senate GOP PAC putting $14 million to support incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas.

President Donald Trump also announced new rules to lower the record-high price of diesel at a rally in Nebraska this week, the biggest single point of frustration for many farmers. The administration also announced new rules to allow ranchers further ability to process and sell their own meat, after upsetting the group by announcing hundreds of thousands of pounds of below-market-priced beef from Brazil and Argentina.

In the announcement, the FTC touted two previous antitrust actions launched during the Biden administration. In July, the agency and five states settled an antitrust case over Deere & Company’s repair restrictions, which the FTC says secures farmers’ right to repair their own Deere equipment. The FTC also settled with Corteva last month, alongside 12 states, over alleged anticompetitive conduct in pesticides.

Ferguson said on social media that farmers “shouldn’t have to overcome artificial service barriers to keep their farm machinery running, or pay inflated prices for critical equipment.”

“And they shouldn’t suffer retaliation for fixing their own equipment, or shopping around for better prices,” Ferguson wrote.

The move comes the day after the Justice Department and USDA announced a new memorandum of understanding that says competition in the agriculture input sector is one of their highest priorities.
entries.author: Tyler Spence

entries.title: Judge Orders Kennedy Center Renovation Documents Unsealed
entries.summary: The documents were used by the center’s board during an August meeting about whether to close the center’s main building.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Wednesday ordered the Trump administration to make public a presentation used by Kennedy Center officials as they considered closing the building for two years, while allowing the government to propose limited redactions to a separate 163-page renovation plan.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ordered the “Delta Construction Group PowerPoint” unsealed in full and said the administration must propose narrowly tailored redactions to the “JLL Plan” by Oct. 14. Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio Kennedy Center board member who is seeking to halt the center’s closure, will have until Oct. 19 to respond to the proposed redactions.

The documents were used by the Kennedy Center board during an Aug. 13 meeting about whether to close the center’s main building for renovations.

The administration had argued that the JLL Plan contained sensitive information, including floor plans, structural schematics, entrances and exits, and restricted-access areas that could pose a security risk if released publicly.

But Cooper said the government had not overcome the strong presumption of public access to court records. He noted that news organizations had already reported portions of the plan and that the administration itself is relying on it in the case.

The ruling is the latest development in Beatty’s lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s control of the Kennedy Center. Beatty has also sought documents and testimony concerning Trump’s involvement in decisions surrounding the center, while the Justice Department has fought her discovery requests.

The Delta presentation is expected to become public sometime this week. The JLL Plan will follow after the court reviews the administration’s proposed redactions.

entries.title: Judge Weighs Whether to Block Some Trump Truth Social Posts
entries.summary: The platform is charging up to $100,000 a month to get 50-millisecond early access to the president’s posts.
entries.content:
A federal judge questioned Wednesday whether he should block President Donald Trump and the White House from posting official announcements on Truth Social when the social media platform is selling early access to his posts.

U.S. District Judge J. Paul Oetken, at a hearing in New York, dove into whether a 50 millisecond head start for corporate clients and high-frequency trading firms who pay up to $100,000 a month for the Truth API feature made enough of a difference for the courts to step in.

"That suggests that whatever the time difference is, it's valuable," Oetken said. But he also suggested 50 milliseconds is a "negligible delay to any human."

And Oetken also asked whether Trump’s ties to Truth Social’s parent company, Trump Media & Technology Group, are enough of a connection to justify a preliminary injunction against the White House.

"There is an extremely close symbiotic relationship that is unusual," the judge said.

In August, left-leaning news organization The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued the president and argued applying a paywall to public statements violates the First Amendment.

David Schulz, an attorney arguing for those plaintiffs, told Oetken that the API feature puts journalists at a disadvantage because they are behind on ways that alert them about Trump’s posts early enough to get to a story first.

The plaintiffs say the president and top aides use the platform to declare military attacks, fire agency heads and announce major domestic policies — communications that frequently rouse market rallies.

“It's significant enough for people to pay more than $1 million annually to get that information quicker,” Schulz said at the hearing.

Schulz said Trump had “outsourced the White House press office to Truth Social” and the administration had never identified any legitimate government interest in providing better access for those willing to pay.

Brantley Mayers, a Justice Department attorney defending the administration, told the judge that presidents choose their way of communicating with the public, and compared Trump’s social media posts to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s fireside chats and John F. Kennedy’s televised speeches.

The amount of time between when API subscribers receive an alert and when Trump’s posts are made public — the 50 milliseconds — does not cause significant harm to journalists, Mayers said.

Oetken pressed Mayers on how there hasn’t been anything like this situation, where Truth Social is a private company but Trump is the largest shareholder, has exclusive agreements about use of his image and was described by the CEO as the man “on the other end of the phone”

Mayers said there is no evidence that Trump was involved in the creation of the Truth API. "That's the missing piece here," Mayers said.

entries.title: Flight Attendants' Union Flags Safety Concerns Over Trump's Proposed Arch
entries.summary: The union president said the project compounds safety concerns that have gone unaddressed since a deadly crash over the Potomac River killed 67 people in January 2025.
entries.content:
By Gary Fields

The union representing thousands of flight attendants said Wednesday it has safety concerns about President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch that will be on final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Association of Flight Attendants-CWA President Sara Nelson said the 250-foot (76 meter) arch compounds multiple safety concerns that she said have gone unaddressed from a deadly January 2025 crash over the Potomac River that killed 67 people. Nelson also criticized Trump's plan to turn the arch into "a top grade military complex” able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition.

“DCA is already stretched to its limit, we do not need an obstacle taking up space in our flight path,” said Nelson. “Nor should commercial aviation have to dodge military drones, missiles or snipers while attempting to take off or land at Washington National Airport. Safety first always.”

Nelson’s statement on behalf of the union, which represents 55,000 flight attendants across 20 airlines, joins the voices of an assemblage of veterans’ groups, Congress members and others with safety concerns and complaints about the memorial's threat to historic and symbolic sightlines between different landmarks in Washington, D.C.

Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.

Last month, the Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the “strong request” of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall (76-meter) memorial arch “into a top grade Military Complex.”

The Federal Aviation Administration said last month before Trump's announcement on it becoming a military complex that the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft, but it should be “appropriately marked with a non-standard eternal flame on top of the structure and floodlight projectors pointed towards the arch to make it noticeable for pilots.

An assessment by the National Park Service said the memorial arch could disrupt the historical significance of dozens of nearby sites. The Park Service approved the project despite its assessment.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced early last month that excavation work on the site in Memorial Circle would begin within weeks. The Interior Department did not respond immediately to questions on the status of that work.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Turning Point USA Is Spending Millions to Boost One of the Last Candidates Endorsed by Charlie Kirk
entries.summary: Republican Andy Biggs is locked in a tight race against Gov. Katie Hobbs in Turning Point’s backyard.
entries.content:
Turning Point USA’s Arizona state PAC has spent a record amount of money on ads to knock Arizona’s Democratic governor out of office.

The PAC has dropped more than $18 million on media buys supporting Rep. Andy Biggs, the Republican nominee for governor, and attacking Gov. Katie Hobbs, according to state campaign finance records reviewed by The Washington Sun. Biggs was one of the last candidates endorsed by Charlie Kirk, the Turning Point founder who lived in Arizona before his assassination last year.

In response to emailed questions from The Sun, a Turning Point spokesperson said the group is focused on Arizona because that’s where it’s headquartered and because it’s “one of the most important states for Republicans in 2028.”

“There are many people on the Left that hope we fail, however we are simply focused on turning out our own base turnout operation,” the spokesperson said in the email. “We do not dabble much in persuasion, only making sure our own voters get the information and turnout to vote.”

The state PAC spent roughly $270,000 on the gubernatorial race in 2022, according to Arizona records, a race where Hobbs narrowly defeated Kari Lake. But this year, the group has leaned in, spending at least $14 million in ads in September alone and adding two $1.7 million ad buys and other five-figure media hits at the start of October.

The group didn’t share additional information in response to a written question about spending not reflected in finance records, the most recent of which only cover ad spending. PACs in Arizona must report ad buys of more than $50,000 within three days, with additional reporting requirements for every additional $25,000 beyond that.

Kirk announced his endorsement of Biggs in May 2025 on “The Charlie Kirk Show,” and he later gave a speech at a Phoenix rally supporting Biggs’ campaign.

“We are fully endorsing my friend Andy Biggs,” Kirk said on his podcast. “Andy, we are behind you 100%, and we’re excited to make you the next governor of the state of Arizona.”

The Cook Political Report has rated the gubernatorial race as “lean Democrat.”

GOP strategist and Phoenix native Barrett Marson told The Sun that the Biggs campaign is “somewhat flailing” in the run-up to November and that Turning Point’s role in the race could become a “lightning rod.” Earlier this year, when Turning Point waded into a typically sleepy statewide utility-board election, voters responded in record turnout by electing a pro-clean energy majority.

“If Andy Biggs loses, Turning Point loses,” Marson said. “That hurts them probably with donors, their image.”

He said Turning Point’s investment in a tough race for Republicans could hurt the group’s chances of becoming an influential voice in future campaign cycles.

“They are trying to expand nationwide, to be an alternative, if you will, to the RNC,” Marson said. “They’re trying to almost become their own national party, really.”

A source familiar with the Biggs campaign said it is grateful for the spending provided by Turning Point and other groups because it’s a “very difficult race.”

A spokesperson for Hobbs’ campaign dismissed the PAC’s spending as an eleventh-hour “bailout.”

“After Republicans have sounded the alarm for weeks about Biggs' floundering campaign, this 15 million dollar bailout from Kari Lake's allies will not change Biggs’ toxic record that is too extreme for Arizona,” Michael Beyer, the campaign spokesperson, said in a statement.

Turning Point has also spent money to support other Arizona Republicans in down-ballot races, including the candidates in the secretary of state and attorney general races.

The Democratic Governors Association committed $10 million in the summer to support Hobbs, while the Republican Governors Association has yet to spend money on behalf of Biggs. The RGA did not comment.
entries.author: Ellie Fivas, Hunter Riggall

entries.title: Forget 'Kids' — At the Trump Accounts Event, They're 'Shareholders'
entries.summary: As nearly every American child is now auto-enrolled in an investment account, the president and his allies treat seeding their economic future like an earnings call.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced Wednesday that every eligible child in America has been automatically enrolled in a federal investing account. But in touting the initiative at an Oval Office event, the president and his allies gave the impression those kids spend more time in a boardroom than a classroom — referring to them as “owners,” “shareholders” and “capitalists.”

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who championed the project, turned to the sixth- and seventh-graders present in the Oval Office and inventoried their holdings.

"You're going to be owners. You guys now own part of Apple. You own part of Dell computers. You own part of McDonald's," he said.

The program, Cruz said, is "creating a whole new generation of capitalists."

He suggested children tell family members to skip the "ugly sweater" for their birthdays and put $50 into their accounts instead.

The investment accounts for minors, written into the tax code as section 530A and launched July 4, are branded Trump Accounts in the app parents must use to claim them. The Treasury Department has opened one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, with over 60 million created automatically.

Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, said having an investment account means that each child "owns a share in one of the biggest popular companies in America." The takeaway, he said, is that "when the U.S. wins, they win too."

IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank Bisignano, who also leads the Social Security Administration, described the program as a venture. "This is a start-up that will have 70 million children in it," he said, adding that its operators "have access to every family in America."

Bisignano said over 10 million accounts were funded with $4.5 billion, figures he expects to reach 25 million accounts and $7 billion by the weekend. That is "25 million American children who now have a piece of capitalism," he said.

Much of that money is from the Dell family. Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell said he and his wife, Susan Dell, had funded 10 million accounts at $250 apiece and would hit the 25 million mark in the coming days, fulfilling a $6.25 billion pledge.

"These children will grow up as owners," Dell said Wednesday.

The Dell money goes to children born between 2016 and 2024 who live in ZIP codes where the median household income falls below $115,000, according to the Invest America website.

Family, friends and employers cannot add anything until a parent claims the account through the app, and nothing can be withdrawn until the child turns 18.

The $1,000 federal deposit is only available for citizen children born between 2025 and 2028, and a parent must claim the account before the child can receive it.

The announcement lands four weeks before the midterms. The Trump Accounts represent the third promise of money to Americans the White House has publicized in recent weeks, after $500 refunds to roughly 1 million people the administration says were overcharged under the Affordable Care Act during the Biden administration, and a proposed $5,000 dividend contingent on Republicans retaining control of Congress.

Trump said the children "are now, and they will be in the future, extremely rich," and are "going to be riding the markets."
entries.author: Ayah Ali-Ahmad

entries.title: Arizona Congressional Candidate Says She Was Raped While Repairing Campaign Signs
entries.summary: The Maricopa County Sheriff's investigation is ongoing.
entries.content:
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office is investigating a sexual assault reported by Bernadette Greene-Placentia, the Democratic nominee for Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, who said she was attacked this summer while she was repairing campaign signs.

Greene-Placentia’s account and a police report were first reported by Phoenix New Times on Wednesday. According to Greene-Placentia, the assault happened around 2 a.m. in a parking lot in Sun City.

The candidate said she was hit over the head and later woke up to find a man on top of her, sexually assaulting her. She said two men were involved in the attack. She said she heard one mumble something she concluded was “Democratic bitch,” though she told the New Times she wasn’t sure that was exactly what he said.

Greene-Placentia said she told her husband and others about the attack two weeks before reporting it to the sheriff's office. The incident report was taken on Aug. 31. She told the New Times she initially did not want to report the attack because she was “embarrassed” and wanted to “forget it happened.”

A department spokesperson told The Washington Sun they would not comment on the incident because the investigation is ongoing. They also said the police report would not be available until after the investigation is complete.

Greene-Placentia told the New Times she had been wearing a campaign T-shirt at the time. Several of her family members, friends and campaign staff said she told them about the attack, with many of them noticing her unusual absence after the assault.

“I just tried to console her in any way I could,” Craig Beckman, Greene-Placentia’s director of communications, told the New Times. “I spent quite a lot of time explaining to her that this isn’t her fault. Just because she put herself in a vulnerable position doesn’t give a man an excuse to physically or sexually assault her.”

The campaign acknowledged The Sun’s request for comment but did not immediately respond to the inquiry.

Greene-Placentia will face Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh in November.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona) shared his support for Greene-Placentia on social media Wednesday, saying he is “absolutely heartbroken to hear this news.”

“We cannot tolerate political or sexual violence in any form. Those responsible must be held accountable,” Gallego wrote on X. “Thank you for speaking out, Bernadette. We're with you.”

Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Arizona) also expressed her support for Greene-Placentia in a post on X, saying “no one should ever have to experience such a horrific act of sexual violence.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Republicans Are Moving Big Money to Red States and Abandoning North Carolina
entries.summary: Top leaders scramble to protect incumbents who are facing increasingly competitive races.
entries.content:
The Republican triage effort is underway.

Senate GOP leaders kick-started the decision to shift resources, all but conceding the North Carolina Senate race as they face the need to shore up other contested races as their majority comes under increasing threat.

Instead, party leaders are plowing funds into Kansas and South Carolina — two reliably red states where the battlefield has expanded amid President Donald Trump’s bottom-of-the-barrel approval ratings and rising costs that have put the party on the back foot.

Although Republicans are still leaning on a map that is largely on favorable ground, they concede that these latest moves are ominous.

“You have conservative states with problems that can be fixed. Even in a bad environment, they’re solvable if you're able to get the rural Republican base to show up. That's pretty much where the cycle is at this point,” said one Republican operative involved in Senate races. “If you cannot get the base to show up, these states … are probably gone.”

This operative, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that “if the map were a bunch of battleground states, it would be a very, very bad night for Republicans.” Rattling off the handful of states the majority runs through, the GOP operative conceded, “[but] if you're talking about South Carolina, then the majority is already gone, so you're just then talking about the cushion.”

The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, reserved $35 million in North Carolina, but it’s pulling out of the state as former Gov. Roy Cooper holds a sizable advantage over Republican Michael Whatley. 

Instead the PAC is dropping $14 million into Kansas to boost Sen. Roger Marshall and $5 million into South Carolina to aid Sen. Darline Graham, with the aim of shoring up the pair of incumbents.

In Kansas, Marshall has found himself in a real race against Democrat Adam Hamilton, with polls showing them in a margin-of-error battle despite the state’s deep-red hue. On top of SLF resources, the Club for Growth also plowed nearly a half-million dollars into the race to help Marshall.

Marshall has faced intense attacks over his state residency and his family beach house in Florida.

Those criticisms are also coming from fellow Republicans, who accuse him of taking the race for granted.

“He's brought a lot of this on himself. This is how races are lost — not taking your campaign seriously,” the operative said. “Living in Florida? … People aren't stupid.”

Marshall has tried to push back, telling The Washington Examiner that he and his wife recently sold their Florida home and that he’s in Kansas for up to 150 days a year when he’s not working in Washington.

The Power to the People PAC, a Democratic group, added $3 million into the Kansas race in recent days, upping its total investment to $6 million.

Ultimately, operatives believe the new GOP spending will stem Democratic momentum, much as it did in 2014 when former Sen. Pat Roberts warded off a last minute charge by Greg Orman. But it will be costly.

South Carolina has become a new sore spot. Annie Andrews, the Democratic candidate, has pulled even with Graham, according to multiple surveys.

The problems largely stem from Graham’s sudden emergence in the state. She was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, and then won a special election in a matter of weeks. Operatives were also quick to note that outside groups also spent to prop up the late Sen. Graham during the final weeks of the 2020 contest against Jaime Harrison, a well-funded challenger. Graham ultimately defeated Harrison by a double-digit margin.

The South Carolina race also garnered the attention of Trump, who derided the Democratic candidate as a “trannie” multiple times in a TruthSocial post. Andrews is not transgender.

“[Andrews] is not for South Carolina, and South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her,” Trump wrote.

Andrews sidestepped the barb, saying she will “work with anyone to put South Carolina first.”

SLF has also made buys in a handful of other states. The group dropped an additional $8 million into Maine to support Sen. Susan Collins, who’s in the midst of a grueling stretch of four debates over 10 days with Democrat Troy Jackson. Despite the rightward tilt of the map, the race has remained one of the preeminent toss-ups.

“It’s weird, for sure. And it doesn’t entirely make sense,” one Democratic operative who’s worked on Senate races said when asked about the Maine race amid the shifting map impacting other Republican incumbents. “Jackson is not a blank canvas, like early-days Platner was. He has a long governing record in the state, for better and worse, and he just seems to have not hit his stride as a statewide candidate.”

In addition, SLF plopped $4 million in Alaska, where Sen. Dan Sullivan is trying to survive a challenge from former Rep. Mary Peltola, and $2 million into Michigan to back former Rep. Mike Rogers against Abdul El-Sayed. The group has now spent $21 million and $53 million in the two states, respectively.

Thune’s Republican PAC also announced eight-figure spends in Iowa and Ohio last week, both of which are central to majority hopes on both sides of the aisle.

While Georgia could be next on the chopping block, there are reasons to keep spending there despite Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff holding a commanding lead over Republican Rep. Mike Collins — namely to boost Republican Rick Jackson in the governor’s race.

Jackson, who has spent heavily out of his own pocket, is in a margin-of-error battle with former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate. The prospect of him winning is a major incentive for groups to continue investing in the state.

“You can’t afford to [pull out] if you’re the Republican outside world. We have the luxury of more money, so we need to be spending in places like that,” a second Republican operative involved in Senate races said. “If we were dealing with the resources or the Democrats are, we’d have been out of Georgia a long time ago.”

Overall, Republican groups have reserved $35 million on the Ossoff-Collins race, including more than $14 million by SLF. The group is slated to spend another $10 million in the coming weeks.

Whether that money sticks remains a major question, especially as the party looks to patch up problem spots.

“You have to stay agile,” said a third Republican operative involved in Senate races. “These are decisions the outside groups don't enjoy making, but when you’re defending this many races, every dollar counts.”
entries.author: Al Weaver

entries.title: Three More Political Committees Struck by Fraudsters
entries.summary: Citizens Against AIPAC Corruption is among the latest victims in a series of political thefts and embezzlements.
entries.content:
Three more political action committees have experienced incidents of fraud, becoming the latest victims in a series of recent thefts, embezzlements and bogus purchases afflicting federal political groups.

Citizens Against AIPAC Corruption, an organization dedicated to shaming politicians and candidates that have taken money linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee or other pro-Israel groups, reported an “external card fraud” worth $2,835.10. An unidentified person spent the money on a purchase with event ticket outlet StubHub, the committee told the Federal Election Commission.

The fraudulent transaction, dated July 8, was “Disputed with the bank,” Citizens Against AIPAC Corruption told federal regulators. Citizens Against AIPAC Corruption, like many other Democratic or left-leaning groups, banks with Amalgamated Bank.

In a September filing, the PAC reported that the money had been reimbursed following the bank dispute on Aug. 18. In a recent letter to the committee, the FEC requested “any further clarifying information” about the “apparent unauthorized disbursement of Committee funds.”

The Democratic Party of Oregon reported a “Fraudulent Credit Card Purchase” of $495 that was spent on Amazon.com on Aug. 24. The funds were refunded two days later, per the filing.

The political action committee for the Pinnacle West Capital Corporation, an S&P 500 utility company that owns Arizona Public Service, reported a “Fraudulent Transaction” worth $3,500.

“The PAC identified an unauthorized bank transaction in August,” the PAC said in a September filing. “Any refund will be reported once the funds are credited back to the PAC bank account.”

The three PACs did not return requests for comment. The unauthorized and fraudulent transactions follow other thefts against PACs reported earlier this year.

In July, the PAC tied to the law firm Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP told federal regulators that some political contribution checks had been stolen from mailboxes in D.C., and the thieves altered the values of the paper checks. The law firm said it recouped the stolen funds, which amounted to $40,000.

That same month, The Washington Sun reported that the Democratic National Committee had been scammed out of nearly $29,000 in February 2025 after a staffer received an email from someone pretending to be the newly elected DNC Chair Ken Martin.

In August, the National Republican Congressional Committee said an unknown actor stole more than $16,300 that was intended to reach a vendor. The NRCC told The Sun that it was working with the authorities to recoup the funds.

Political committees for Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey), Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) and accounting giant KPMG have also been hit by thieves in recent months.
entries.author: Mark Alfred

entries.title: Bowser’s Plan for a Massive Spa Along the Anacostia River May Be Dead
entries.summary: Janeese Lewis George, her likely successor, is against the proposed deal for Poplar Point.
entries.content:
An ambitious plan pitched by Mayor Muriel Bowser for a 500,000-square-foot spa and waterpark complex on the banks of the Anacostia River is unlikely to move forward in the D.C. Council, after Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George — who is poised to succeed her as the District’s mayor — said she opposes the project.

“I have concerns regarding the proposed development project at Poplar Point, which is one of the East Coast's last great urban waterfront redevelopment opportunities,” Lewis George said in a text message to The Washington Sun. “This is prime waterfront real estate that should be used to leverage the building of more affordable homes and the creation of good jobs. The current proposal does neither. We must make this a better deal for District residents.”

The clash between Bowser and Lewis George has to do both with the particular details of the project and with their competing interests: Bowser is looking to cement her legacy with development deals, some that have been years in the making, while Lewis George is looking for opportunities to enact her own priorities once she takes office Jan. 2.

One place that offers chances for both is Poplar Point, the 110-acre plot of riverfront land between the Frederick Douglass and 11th Street bridges and located across the Anacostia River from Nationals Park. Long owned by the federal government, in 2006 Congress ordered that Poplar Point be turned over to D.C. for local use.

The slow-going process picked up steam in recent years, and in 2025 Bowser announced the selection of Therme, an Austrian operator of health and wellness centers — large-scale spas, in effect — to build its first U.S. location on 15 acres at the site. (There’s another site in development in Dallas.) She pitched the project — which was expected to cost $500 million to build — as a new destination for an underserved side of the river.

“Not only will it create jobs and opportunity, it will serve as a catalyst for economic growth along the Anacostia waterfront,” she said at the time. “This is a unique opportunity for D.C. and an economic driver for Ward 8 — creating jobs, attracting visitors and delivering new opportunities for our residents.”

Therme officials spent the last few years working to build local support for their project, hiring a former chief of staff for Ward 8 council member Trayon White to serve as its community lead, hosting a pop-up sauna village in Ward 8, and flying community leaders and local influencers to Romania to see the company’s flagship spa. Therme gained support from dozens of individuals and organizations in Ward 8, including the Anacostia Coordinating Council, Martha’s Table and the United Planning Organization.

Bowser submitted two bills to the council last month dealing with Poplar Point. One would finalize the transfer of the site from federal to local control, which includes a series of land swaps to facilitate the move of the U.S. Park Police headquarters from Poplar Point to Joint Base Anacostia Bolling. The second bill spelled out the terms of the Therme deal, turning over a 15-acre portion to the company for $1 in annual rent for 20 years and a commitment that the spa would be built within six years.

Those bills accompanied five other proposed development deals, including the redevelopment of the Frank D. Reeves Center on U Street into housing and a new headquarters for the NAACP; the construction of a new library and recreation center with housing on top in Chevy Chase; and affordable housing, retail, and health care services at the former Fletcher-Johnson school in Ward 7.

“The local real estate market remains volatile, and investors are extremely cautious in their investment decisions,” Bowser wrote to lawmakers in mid-September. “Approval of these bills provides them with the certainty they need for these projects to advance. Given the last financial impacts of the DOGE cuts on our local economy — including the loss of tens of thousands of jobs — we must not lose momentum on diversifying our economy and creating jobs for our residents.”

Still, Lewis George’s skepticism with Poplar Point seemed evident last week, when Tommy Wells, a former council member and mayoral hopeful who is now chairing her campaign, posted his thoughts on the projects on X. “This is a mistake and unneeded,” he wrote. “Valuable riverfront land should be used for housing. Council should oppose it.”

Bowser’s dump of legislation on the council in the final months of its two-year legislative calendar — when lawmakers rush to pass their own bills — also struck some of them as the outgoing mayor being naively hopeful, if not somewhat deaf to the political reality that Lewis George is likely to be D.C.’s next mayor. (She faces nominal opposition in the November general election.)

“The presumptive winner of the November election is a council member right now and I expect she’s going to do the same thing Muriel did when she was first elected: ‘I don’t want things going through, it should wait until I become mayor,’” said D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson, referring to Bowser’s first election to the city’s top office in 2014 as she served on the council.

“It’s almost like not taking the legislative process seriously to wait this long,” Mendelson added, “that the council doesn’t need to hear from the public, the council just needs to approve this, which is disrespecting why we’re here.”

Beyond being the likely next mayor, Lewis George also plays a critical role in Bowser’s development deals: She chairs the council committee that handles many proposed uses of public land for private development. In a text message exchange with The Sun, Lewis George confirmed that she wouldn’t hold a hearing on the Poplar Point bills, effectively killing them for the time being.

“Wait until next year in some capacity,” she wrote.

Bowser’s office declined to comment. In an emailed statement, Therme USA Executive Chairman John Alschuler pledged to continue working to make the project a reality.

“Therme D.C. represents a generational opportunity to bring significant private investment to Ward 8, while helping to unlock Poplar Point as a vibrant waterfront neighborhood with housing and other mixed uses,” he wrote. “We have worked closely with the community to build broad support and shape a project that delivers meaningful benefits for the people who live here, including permanent jobs, opportunities for local businesses, expanded access to health and well-being, and a 70-acre world-class public park. We look forward to continuing to share that vision and our commitment to the District.”

It’s not all bad news for Bowser’s other deals, though.

Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin will hold hearings this month on the Fletcher-Johnson proposal and a move to redevelop the Georgetown Boathouse, and next month will hold a separate hearing on the Chevy Chase library project. Lewis George says she will hold her own hearing, indicating that the long-awaited project could be approved by the council this year.

entries.title: Judge Accuses ICE of Falsifying Documents to Cover Up Illegal Arrests
entries.summary: The Trump-appointed judge wrote that the agents’ testimony bears “all the hallmarks of coordinated fabrication.”
entries.content:
A federal judge in New York this week accused Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents of falsifying records to cover up a pair of erroneous arrests, including one that resulted in significant injury to a U.S. citizen.

Judge Gary R. Brown of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York issued the scathing reprimand Monday, condemning the agents’ actions when they apparently misidentified a pair of men they arrested in New York City earlier this year — then allegedly covered their tracks by falsifying official paperwork.

“The evidence suggests that ICE attempted to support their unsupported misidentification argument through false or misleading documentation and testimony,” Brown, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, wrote in a 28-page ruling, determining that the “arrest and detention of petitioner were illegal.”

The petitioner, Angel Jesus Almonte, a 26-year-old undocumented immigrant, alleges ICE agents arrested him based on a physical description despite the fact that he’s five inches shorter and 80 pounds lighter than their intended target, the filing says.

In June, Almonte filed an emergency habeas petition challenging his arrest, detention and the conditions of his confinement, the filing says.

During cross-examination, the ICE team leader acknowledged, “It’s very easy to see they’re two different people.”

Following the arrest, Brown determined that the paperwork filed by agents contained false information, as did testimony provided by the officials.

The case stems from a May 6 ICE operation in which three officers were involved: team leader John Katepodis, deportation officer Kevin Brodowsky and deportation officer Zamir Yassin, all relatively new to their jobs, Brown wrote.

At the time of the arrests, the agents said they were searching for an undocumented immigrant with a criminal record, as well as a second person without any known convictions. They claimed to have spotted Almonte — whom they mistook for one of their targets — conduct a drug deal outside of a building in the Bronx, though officers also wrote in a report that Almonte was not in possession of drugs or money at the time of his arrest.

Brown later determined that agents had falsified a warrant following the arrest to justify their apparent instance of mistaken identity, and only after detaining Almonte did they determine he was in the country illegally.

“ICE agents prepared a substantially false administrative warrant in an attempt to rationalize their actions,” Brown wrote, adding that the agents’ claim that they had witnessed a drug transaction “bear all the hallmarks of coordinated fabrication.”

The agents then made another arrest on the same block, claiming to have found their second target. That man, 19-year-old Jeury Concepción, is a U.S. citizen who said officers did not ask to see his identification before taking him to the ground. He was injured during the encounter and received stitches for a deep cut he sustained on the side of his head.

The agents also claimed that the incident was a case of mistaken identity.

Joshua Dayan, a lawyer for Concepción, told The New York Times that he planned to sue ICE and the agents involved.

“What happened to him should not happen to anybody … let alone a U.S. citizen,” Dayan said. “All they did was run up to Jeury and attack him.”

Trump nominated Brown to the court in 2018, and the Senate confirmed him by voice vote the following year. A former federal magistrate, Brown was first appointed to the Eastern District of New York in 2015 by then-President Barack Obama but never confirmed by the Senate before his nomination expired.

Brown has been an outspoken critic of Trump’s immigration crackdown.

In a 2025 ruling reported by Courthouse News Service, Brown threatened the Department of Homeland Security with contempt after the department refused to provide his court with photos of a Long Island holding room, which he said had been maintained “in a manner that shocks the conscience.”

In Monday’s ruling, Brown ordered ICE to explain what disciplinary procedures it would hand down to the agents and any steps it plans to undertake to prevent any similar incidents in the future. He also left open the threat of penalties, including contempt charges, for agency officials.

entries.title: Trump Ally Rogers Calls for an End to President’s Trade War With Canada
entries.summary: Trump says the Republican Senate nominee's new ad is simply a call for Canada to cut a deal.
entries.content:
Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers is the latest Republican to break from President Donald Trump, calling for the end of the "tariff war” with Canada in an ad launched Wednesday, less than a month before midterms.

“Here in Michigan we know Canada is not our enemy,” Rogers says in the ad. “We need to end this tariff war now.”

In July, Trump imposed a 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods, including cars, alcohol and dairy products. The levies were meant to offset “the burden and disadvantage on U.S. commerce from Canada’s discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce,” according to the White House

Canada launched counter-tariffs that matched the White House’s last month.

The ad marks a shift in Rogers’ position. As recently as last month, Reuters reported, the Michigan Republican called the tariffs “necessary.”

When asked about Rogers’ ad, Trump said he viewed the video as a call for Canada to make a deal.

“Canada has been ripping off our country for many, many years,” Trump said Wednesday. “We don't need Canada for anything.”

Rogers is facing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in a hotly contested race for an open Senate seat held by Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, who is retiring.

With just weeks to go until Election Day, candidates across the country are trying to convince voters they can help stem Americans’ cost-of-living struggles. And Trump’s plummeting approval rating isn’t helping Republicans’ case.

“Prices are too high…” Rogers wrote in the social media post that features the tariff ad. “In the Senate, I’ll bring both parties together to lower costs and put Michigan families first.”

American households will see cost increases of about $1,100 a year from the tariffs, according to the Yale Budget Lab.

This isn’t the first time Rogers has seemingly broken with the president this election cycle — nor is he the first Republican to move away from Trump on some issues. Last month, Rogers called for an end to the Iran war. Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton said in a leaked audio clip that Trump's war — and the rising fuel prices that resulted — were hurting Republicans, and Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Florida) released an ad criticizing Trump’s immigration enforcement.

El-Sayed reshared Rogers’ post Wednesday with a pointed rebuttal.

“You cheerled this tariff war from the beginning and you’re flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall,” El-Sayed wrote. “Donald is the reason we’re in a trade war. And he’s the reason you’re running.”

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Choosin’ Texas? I Can’t Tell
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Oct. 7, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Donald Trump is descending on Texas for the fourth time in six weeks — this time to San Antonio. The president made one trip to the state during the 2018 midterm stretch, Houston Chronicle reporter Jeremy Wallace notes.

  • The leaks keep coming: Ken Paxton told donors and lobbyists he believes the war in Iran and high gas prices have hurt his campaign, Axios reported this morning. Last week, he was recorded saying the president’s Dallas midterm convention had “dropped our numbers.”
  • But Trump continues to stand behind his pick: “I think he’ll be a great senator,” he told reporters in the Oval Office, adding that “I would have no regrets at all” about the endorsement.
Meanwhile, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and the Democratic Governors Association are each sending $1 million to boost Gina Hinojosa in her quest to unseat Gov. Greg Abbott, per The New York Times.

  • Abbott’s reported cash on hand still dwarfs hers by about $14 million, according to yesterday’s fundraising reports — but that’s after he burned through $141.3 million since the start of this year.




THE WHITE HOUSE

Trump says he’s looking into reports that two political advisers performed consulting work for a pro-Russian nationalist government in Bosnia-Herzegovina, suggesting he may fire both longtime confidants if there is a conflict of interest.

Trump wants to build a permanent Camp David-style presidential retreat at his golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida — and the county is seriously considering the proposal.

Pete Hegseth greeted thousands of sailors returning from a record-setting deployment aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln by saying, in prepared remarks, that media reports had overstated the problems they faced aboard the carrier.





THE AGENCIES

The FCC is considering a conservative group’s request to loosen rules on political robocalls, including those with AI-generated voices, before the midterms.

The EPA plans to roll back regulations on methane emissions and other greenhouse gases for the oil and gas industry, administrator Lee Zeldin announced today.

U.S. officials warned Russia in a confidential diplomatic communication that it was failing to comply with global health obligations by not sharing details about the death of a plague researcher in Siberia.





THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Hillary Clinton endorsed her first candidate of the 2026 election cycle this week: Minnesota Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan, who is the state’s lieutenant governor.

Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers called for an end to the “tariff war” with Canada in a new campaign advertisement, Politico reports, marking another Republican break from Trump weeks before the midterms.





THE COURTS

The DNC is suing Trump’s administration over its recent TV ads made using taxpayer dollars.

A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to make public a presentation Kennedy Center officials used as they considered closing the building for two years. The ruling also allows the government to propose limited redactions to a separate 163-page renovation plan.
